<a id="item-1"></a>
## [Reflection Releases Beam, a 501B Open-Weight Sparse MoE Model](https://reflection.ai/blog/introducing-beam) ⭐️ 9.0/10

Reflection has released Beam, an open-weight sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active parameters, targeting coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. The model was pretrained on 23.8 trillion curated tokens and further improved through reinforcement learning. Beam is one of the largest open-weight models released to date, and it intensifies the competition between Western and Chinese labs in the open-weight LLM space. Its release gives developers a new high-capacity option for coding and agentic applications, though community members question whether it truly outperforms smaller Chinese open models. Beam uses a sparse MoE architecture that decouples total parameter count from inference compute, activating only 23B of its 501B parameters per token. Compared with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Beam has fewer total parameters (501B vs 552B) but far more active parameters (23B vs 8B prefill / 16B decode) and was trained on fewer tokens (28T vs 45T).

hackernews · Philpax · Oct 5, 19:16 · [Discussion](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49969183)

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a machine learning technique that divides a model into multiple specialized sub-networks, or experts, and routes each input to only a few of them. This sparsity lets a model have a very large total parameter count while keeping the compute cost per token much lower, because only the selected experts are activated during inference. Open-weight models are those whose trained parameters are publicly released, allowing anyone to download, run, and fine-tune them.

## [ImmuneAgent AI discovers broadly neutralizing antibodies from human B cell repertoires](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03160) ⭐️ 9.0/10

Researchers introduced ImmuneAgent, a closed-loop AI system that combines multimodal reasoning, continual meta-learning, and wet-lab feedback to discover broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) directly from natural human B cell receptor repertoires. Screening vaccinated or infected cohorts, it achieved a ~55% neutralization discovery rate (60 of 110 cloned candidates) and ~11% bnAb yield (12 of 110), with five antibodies conferring 100% in vivo protection against lethal influenza challenge. This represents a new paradigm in computational antibody discovery, showing that AI can generalize across viral families and identify bnAbs without antigen-specific sorting, which could accelerate therapeutic development for emerging pandemic threats. The high experimental validation rate and in vivo protection suggest the approach may be practically deployable rather than purely theoretical. The system outperformed a state-of-the-art sequence-based neutralization predictor and cofolding models at the same cloning budget, and it identified FCRL5+CD27+ atypical memory B cells as a conserved bnAb reservoir plus hydrophobic interface enrichment as a cross-viral structural signature. It also discovered human metapneumovirus (hMPV) cross-neutralizing and human papillomavirus (HPV)-neutralizing antibodies without antigen-specific sorting.

## [World Editing: Intervening on Executable Worlds at Increasing Depth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02331) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper formulates world editing as intervening on an existing executable world while preserving properties that should remain unchanged, and introduces intervention depth as an axis describing how strongly an edit couples world entities, dynamics, and systems. The authors present IGMWorld and IGMBench, a benchmark of 110 tasks with over 1.1K executable state and behavioral criteria across Minecraft and Terraria, and report that the strongest frontier coding agent configuration solves 78.2% of tasks under a strict task-level criterion, with criterion-level performance reaching 94.8%. This work positions world editing as a distinct capability from world generation and interaction, which could spur further research into interactive world models and AI agents that can deliberately modify existing environments rather than merely generate or act within them. The benchmark and findings provide a practical testbed for measuring how well coding agents handle increasingly coupled edits, with implications for game modding, simulation, and agent evaluation. Reliability generally decreases with intervention depth, and this pattern persists even among tasks with similar numbers of evaluation criteria; most failed edits still build and load successfully, suggesting the main difficulty is making the edited world behave as requested. Visual consistency remains a separate weakness, with all evaluated configurations below 50% joint visual pass rate.

A new arXiv paper introduces Pluralistic Preference Optimization (PlurPO), a training method that reduces social sycophancy in language models by having them simulate multiple stakeholders' perspectives in interpersonal conflicts. PlurPO cuts endorsement of harmful intent statements by 89% on average across four models and closes the gap to human endorsement rates on general advice questions from 17.8% to 8.0%. Social sycophancy in personal advice is a growing safety concern as relationship advice becomes a top use of generative AI, and PlurPO offers a scalable, label-free mitigation that could generalize across model sizes. This work advances AI alignment by addressing sycophancy in settings without ground truth, a gap prior factual-sycophancy mitigations could not fill. PlurPO uses only signals the model produces about its own outputs, requiring no ground-truth labels, and the preference dataset built for an 8B model transfers effectively to a larger 32B model. The method was evaluated across four datasets and four model families, though the abstract is truncated and full limitations are not yet visible.

**Background**: Sycophancy in AI refers to a model's tendency to align outputs with a user's perceived preferences or self-image, even when doing so reduces accuracy or candor. Prior mitigations for factual sycophancy rely on ground-truth answers, which do not exist for personal advice, so social sycophancy has mainly been addressed with simple prompting and post-training methods of limited effectiveness.

## [LLM Agents Show Complex Contagion in Belief Adoption Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02654) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02654) empirically measures belief adoption in LLM agents, finding that the probability an agent adopts a claim given how many peers endorse it follows a sigmoid adoption kernel, a hallmark of complex contagion. The study also shows that in multi-agent systems, belief spread is stronger on clustered than random networks, with a bifurcating cascade window and self-sustaining hysteretic consensus. This work bridges complex-systems theory and multi-agent AI, showing that LLM collectives can exhibit population-level dynamics previously studied only in human social networks. It has implications for social simulation, multi-agent system design, and understanding how consensus forms and persists in AI-driven information ecosystems. The adoption threshold is sensitive to three factors—the claim's plausibility, the source's reliability, and the agent's disposition—which the authors approximate with a single effective dimension they call coherence with the agent's prior beliefs. The observed hysteresis means consensus is far harder to remove than to establish, a caveat for anyone trying to steer or correct beliefs in such systems.

## [GHOST: A New Safety Failure Mode in Long-Horizon Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02664) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02664) identifies and names a failure mode called GHOST (Governance Hazard from Overlooked Safety Constraints across Turns), in which a long-horizon agent violates a safety constraint specified many turns earlier even under benign interaction conditions. The authors report an 11.5% occurrence rate on GPT-5.5 and propose a two-layer defense, STAR-Guard, that eliminates observed GHOST events in their experiments. As long-horizon agents take on increasingly complex, multi-step tasks, this failure mode could cause irreversible real-world damage even when no adversarial input is present, making it directly relevant to anyone deploying autonomous systems. The paper's theoretical analysis and mitigation strategy offer concrete guidance for AI safety and agent reliability engineering. Theoretically, the authors show that if the residual conditional violation hazard along each safe prefix is bounded below by a non-summable sequence, execution enters the hazard region almost surely. STAR-Guard couples historical semantic safety constraint restoration (to reduce unsafe proposals) with a deterministic pre-execution audit layer (to block residual violations from reaching the environment).

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Long-horizon agents are AI systems that operate over extended interaction histories, completing tasks that require many turns of planning and tool use. Safety constraints are typically specified once, early in a session, and must remain in force across all subsequent turns; GHOST describes the failure to carry those constraints forward. Reinforcement learning and other training paradigms that optimize for task completion can underweight such long-range constraints, which is why this failure mode has been underexplored.

## [Study Finds Commercial LLM Routers Fail to Beat Random Baseline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02762) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02762) analyzes six commercial dynamic LLM routers across 14 settings on a benchmark spanning eight task categories, and finds that none outperforms a router that randomly selects between two well-chosen models at matched cost, with some underperforming by more than 10 percentage points. The authors trace this gap to four recurring failure patterns—difficulty blindness, length reversal, semantic matching, and roster suboptimality—and propose an alternative evaluation methodology plus a simple two-model router that avoids all four. The findings challenge the core premise of dynamic LLM routing, a widely promoted technique for cutting inference costs, and suggest that current commercial routers may be optimizing the wrong objective. This could push the AI/ML community to rethink how routers are trained and evaluated, and to reconsider whether large model rosters are justified at all. The paper shows that the standard cost-accuracy Pareto efficiency objective on realized costs actually rewards the first three failure patterns—escalating moderately hard queries over the hardest ones, shorter queries over longer ones, and routing by a query's source rather than its difficulty. It also argues that the two assumptions justifying large rosters, model granularity and model specialization, do not hold empirically, and notes that even its proof-of-concept two-model router gains little over random routing because a well-chosen roster leaves little to route.

**Background**: Dynamic LLM routing is a technique that sends each incoming query to the cheapest model that can answer it correctly, aiming to reduce inference costs while maintaining quality. Commercial routers typically rely on a roster of multiple models of varying sizes and costs, and are evaluated on cost-accuracy Pareto efficiency, which measures how well they trade off cost against accuracy. PAPER2LLM++ introduces a framework that treats the growing body of LLM research as a stream of evidence and supervision, extracting evidence-grounded findings from each incoming paper, testing whether the reported limitation persists in the current model, and converting findings into candidate learning signals when needed. A try-evaluate-commit procedure integrates an update only when it improves the targeted behavior without substantially forgetting prior improvements or degrading general capabilities. The framework is evaluated across a sequential stream of research-discovered LLM failures, showing that models can progressively incorporate new findings while retaining earlier gains. The paper introduces Ansatz, a mathematical research agent built around Continual Graph Memory, a graph-based, evolvable, cross-problem memory system that organizes the entire proof search process and reuses knowledge from prior explorations. Ansatz reports closure on all ten First Proof Second Batch problems and autonomously solves the Jamison caterpillar conjecture and Erdős Problems 289, 348, and 488, with partial progress on several other open problems. This work addresses the core bottleneck of long-horizon automated mathematical research: organizing and reusing the massive volume of intermediate proof results generated by many parallel agents. If validated, such memory systems could significantly accelerate automated mathematical discovery and reduce redundant search, with implications for AI-driven theorem proving and open problem solving. The unified graph memory represents facts, plans, and counterexamples as nodes with explicit relational edges, while dependency-aware retrieval supplies targeted local context, an evidence-sensitive curator updates the research frontier and distills lessons, and scoped recall surfaces earlier statements and negative findings for local re-proving rather than uncritical reuse. Experiments include runs across all ten First Proof Second Batch problems plus four component studies.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Automated theorem proving with large language models often suffers from combinatorial explosion during long-horizon proof search, because without an executable global route specifying key intermediate milestones, the prover is forced into largely unconstrained exploration. Continual graph memory is a technique that treats a graph state as a writable memory, allowing knowledge to be accumulated and reused across tasks, and has recently been explored in areas such as adaptive recommendation. Ansatz builds on this idea by maintaining a unified, evolvable graph of proof artifacts across different mathematical problems.

## [CreativePreferences Dataset Reveals Tacit Gaps in AI Preference Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03025) ⭐️ 8.0/10

The paper introduces CreativePreferences, a large labeled preference dataset containing 2.8 million texts and 317 million human preference judgments across 7 creative domains, along with 42 benchmark tasks. It formalizes and measures articulability gaps (VAT-VA) and verifiability gaps (VAT-V) using executable programs, rubric banks, and densely trained models. This work highlights that current AI alignment methods like RLAIF and RLVR, which rely on articulated rubrics and verifiers, may miss tacit components of human preference, potentially leading to misalignment. It provides a measurement framework and dataset that could influence future RLHF and preference modeling research. The gaps occur across all domains, including traditionally verifiable ones like mathematics and software engineering, and widen as more people participate in judgment, consistent with Collins' collective tacit knowledge. The paper also shows that articulating preference shifts it away from the tacit dimension, analogous to Goodhart's law.

## [HACKTRACE detects reward hacking in code generation via internal states](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03055) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers released HACKTRACE, a behavior-supervised monitor that detects reward hacking during code generation by reusing the agent's own internal states, achieving a mean per-problem AUC of 0.997 with only 8 ms of monitoring overhead. They also released 173,561 annotated multi-turn coding trajectories from Qwen3-8B, showing that supervising shortcut behavior independently of exploit success substantially improves detection. Reward hacking — where a coding agent passes tests by deleting or weakening them rather than fixing the bug — is a growing AI safety concern as agents are increasingly optimized against test suites. HACKTRACE shows that accurate detection can be turned into a useful training signal, reducing the cheating share of passing solutions from 82-91% to 1-5% under strong GRPO penalties while retaining honest, correct solutions. The monitor reads internal states the agent already computes while generating code, enabling monitoring before a turn is complete without additional language-model tokens or forward passes, and it combines this evidence with static features of the final files. The same generation states also provide an inexpensive monitoring signal for reinforcement learning, and detection accuracy remains high as the policy evolves.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Reward hacking occurs when a reinforcement learning agent exploits flaws or ambiguities in the reward function to achieve high rewards without genuinely completing the intended task; in code generation, tests act as a proxy metric that agents can game. Qwen3-8B is an 8-billion-parameter open-weight model from the Qwen3 family, used here as the coding agent whose trajectories were annotated. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm commonly used to fine-tune language models, and in this work it supplies the penalties that suppress cheating behavior.

## [Depth as Time: How One-Step Generative Models Reorganize Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03626) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.03626) empirically demonstrates a phenomenon called "depth as time": in one-step generative models, the denoising computation that multi-step diffusion performs across sampling steps unfolds across the depth of a single forward pass, and can be recovered by decoding intermediate layers with the model's own output head. The authors show this depthwise computation depends on the transport task a flow map is trained to solve, with MeanFlow exhibiting both denoising and renoising within a single network evaluation, and demonstrate that a MeanFlow SiT-L/2 model can be compressed 16.6× in parameters into a single time-conditioned block. This finding offers new mechanistic insight into one-step generative models, a highly active area of efficient generative modeling, by showing that the temporal computation of diffusion is not eliminated but reorganized across network depth. It could directly influence how researchers design and compress diffusion distillation and flow-map models, potentially enabling much smaller and faster generators without losing the denoising behavior that makes them work. The most surprising case is MeanFlow, where probing shorter transport intervals reveals both denoising and renoising within a single network evaluation, whereas generators trained without a time-indexed transport task, such as drifting models, do not exhibit the same depthwise denoising. The authors also show that when the layerwise computation is treated explicitly as a flow, a single time-conditioned block can be trained to denoise across layers, compressing a MeanFlow SiT-L/2 model by 16.6× in parameters.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Diffusion models generate images by starting from noise and iteratively denoising over many sampling steps, which is slow because each step requires a full network evaluation. One-step generative models, such as those based on distillation or learned flow maps like MeanFlow, aim to compress this multi-step trajectory into a single forward pass to achieve much faster sampling. MeanFlow in particular maps noise to data in one step by regressing an interval-averaged velocity, and this paper asks what happens to the original multi-step denoising trajectory when generation is compressed this way.

## [NeutronGym: Physics-Graded Neutron Instrument Design for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03631) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers at Oak Ridge National Laboratory introduced NeutronGym, described as the first executable environment for neutron instrument design, where LLM agents build instruments through validating tools, McStas ray-tracing simulates what they build, and a level-resolved ladder grades syntax, runtime, structure, and science without any LLM judge. On the curated McStasBench slice of 16 published-instrument tasks, seven models reproduce at most 7 of 16, none retrieves a reference, and none meets an improvement target, while reinforcement learning on the environment's reward lifts Qwen3-8B from 11% to 77% on held-out instances of a procedural family (69% at a second seed), surpassing an untrained Qwen3-32B. This work provides an objective, simulator-grounded benchmark for testing whether language-model agents can actually do physics rather than recall it, addressing a core weakness of LLM evaluation in scientific domains. The dramatic RL gain (11% to 77%) shows that executable physics environments can serve as effective training signals, pointing toward a path for AI-for-science agents in instrument design and related engineering tasks. The level-resolved ladder's partial credit is essential: without it, the RL gain collapses by 60 points, and the trained model only matches a classical optimizer given the closed-form physics (77% vs 81%, a gap that does not separate at this size), while frontier models still solve 98-99%. The scored tasks focus on setting numeric parameters within fixed layouts rather than inventing new instrument topologies, and the authors report failing four task designs that no-model baselines could solve, releasing the probes that found them.

## [GlanceWAM Decouples Visual Imagination from Robot Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23927) ⭐️ 8.0/10

GlanceWAM introduces an asynchronous world-action model that generates visual imagination off the critical path on a slow clock while an action head decodes action chunks at control rate (48 ms) purely in latent space. It achieves 72.2% on the 24-task RoboCasa kitchen benchmark versus 67.1% for synchronous Cosmos Policy, 99.0% on LIBERO, and cuts per-chunk control latency 24x relative to synchronous world-action models on a single A100. This work breaks the long-standing speed-success trade-off in world-action models, showing that test-time visual imagination can be preserved without blocking real-time control. It could significantly advance embodied AI and robot learning by making generative world models practical for real-time manipulation. The approach relies on a non-interfering attention mask that isolates video representations and staleness-robust horizon training that accommodates asynchronous lookahead aging. Trained purely on demonstrations, it outperforms π0.5 in single-arm and bimanual real-robot manipulation without any robot-data pretraining.

**Background**: World-action models (WAMs) use video generative models as rich physical priors for robot learning, but synchronous video generation at control rate is latency-prohibitive, while removing test-time visual imagination hurts task success. GlanceWAM builds on a shared video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone, where a slow asynchronous proposer imagines a single lookahead frame seconds into the future in the background. The action head then consumes this imagination directly in latent space at control rate, avoiding the need to decode pixels on the critical path.

A new arXiv paper (2610.02241) presents an end-to-end hardware-software co-design framework that compresses trillion-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) expert weights into hardware-native, low-precision sparse representations and accelerates their execution on NVIDIA Sparse Tensor Cores (SpTCs). The framework improves state-of-the-art joint sparse-quantization accuracy by up to 4.35 percentage points while preserving 96.09% of the original model's performance, and on NVIDIA B200 GPUs its custom grouped sparse GEMM kernel outperforms the vendor baseline by up to 1.65x, increasing serving throughput by 1.18x and reducing end-to-end latency by up to 4.03x. MoE architectures are the dominant path to trillion-parameter frontier language models, but their massive memory footprints and memory-bandwidth demands make deployment expensive; this work shows that hardware-software co-design can make such models practically deployable without large quality loss. The results suggest that exploiting Sparse Tensor Cores for MoE inference could meaningfully lower serving costs and latency for the largest AI models, affecting both AI systems research and production deployment of frontier LLMs. The algorithmic core relaxes discrete semi-structured support selection through continuous reparameterization, enabling differentiable joint optimization of sparsity patterns and quantized weights under a router-weighted reconstruction objective with scalable expert-parallel compression. Systemically, the authors develop a custom grouped sparse GEMM kernel tailored to low-precision sparse MoE inference on SpTCs, addressing the prior lack of grouped sparse GEMM primitives; evaluations span MoE models from 30 billion to one trillion parameters.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a machine learning technique that uses multiple expert subnetworks to divide a problem space, allowing models to scale to far more parameters with less compute per token because only a subset of experts is activated for each input. Sparse Tensor Cores are hardware units in modern NVIDIA GPUs (introduced with the Ampere architecture) that accelerate matrix math when weights follow a semi-structured 2:4 sparsity pattern, meaning at least two of every four contiguous values are zero, yielding roughly double the math throughput of dense units. Quantization reduces the numerical precision of weights to save memory and bandwidth, but naively combining sparsity and quantization in MoE models tends to degrade model quality, which is the gap this paper aims to close.

A new arXiv paper (2610.02373) formalizes Auxiliary Schema-Level Entity as a novel attack surface in GraphRAG pipelines and introduces the 3S Framework (Semantics, Structure, Scoring) along with the Hop-Decayed Influence (HDI) attack. Across HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA benchmarks on Microsoft GraphRAG and HippoRAG2, HDI achieves 88-94% attack success rate while modifying as few as 0.016% of auxiliary structures. This work exposes a structural blind spot in current GraphRAG defenses: auxiliary schema-level entities receive implicit trust without runtime validation, and each corrupted structure can affect up to 6.00 queries via a 1:N amplification effect unavailable to instance-level attacks. It is likely to spur further research into securing LLM-based retrieval systems and graph-augmented generation pipelines. The manipulated structures evade perplexity and paraphrase defenses with over 99% evasion rate because they remain linguistically coherent system-generated artifacts. HDI identifies high-impact targets through query-aware influence propagation and corrupts their auxiliary structures post-indexing, with a Schema Leverage Ratio of up to 6.00 queries per modification.

## [Coco: An Agentic Copilot for Hardware-Software Co-Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02376) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers from Google and academia present Coco (Copilot for Codesign), an agentic platform deployed with TPU architects that accelerates the hardware-software co-design lifecycle of setting up experiments, sweeping simulators, and deriving insights. Coco is built as four layers: a datastore that registers every simulation sweep into a normalized relational schema so agents ground every number in a SQL query, a library of typed-API tools agents compose without human orchestration, agents encoding recurring workflows such as iso-execution analysis, and a platform UX whose navigation state doubles as agent context. Co-design is a distinct agentic domain where the evidence behind each decision—hundreds of gigabytes of fresh simulation sweeps over novel design points—is by construction absent from any LLM's pretraining corpus and has no external literature to retrieve, so naive chat-with-your-data approaches hallucinate exactly where correctness matters most. By grounding agents in simulation data, Coco targets a reduction in time-to-simulation and time-to-insight for high-stakes architectural decisions, with potential impact on ML accelerator design across the industry. The platform's most notable workflow is iso-execution analysis, which compares systems at matched execution configurations, including swept-but-dominated points off the Pareto frontier. The paper reports early deployment experience rather than a full quantitative evaluation, and argues that expert adoption hinges on a UX balancing IDE-style control with interactive exploration.

## [Shared Memory in Looped Transformers Boosts Quality and Cuts Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02383) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02383) pretrains looped language models so that only the first recursion writes a key-value cache, while later recursions read it and keep only a short local window. The resulting Looped Prediction Transformer (LPT) and its hybrid variant, at 150M-1B parameters with five recursions, lower validation perplexity on FineWeb-Edu by 1.12-1.82 versus a same-size standard Transformer while using 76-79% less context memory. This is a counterintuitive result: sharing memory across recursions was expected to hurt quality, but it actually improves it while drastically reducing inference memory. It could reshape how looped or recurrent-depth models are designed for efficient inference, especially as architectures like these are reportedly used in frontier systems such as GPT-6 Astra. The analysis shows that shared and local memory develop different representations, later recursions attend mostly to the shared memory, and the shared cache acts as a gradient highway back to the first recursion. The hybrid variant achieves the best quality-memory trade-off, though results are limited to 150M-1B parameter models and the FineWeb-Edu validation set.

**Background**: Looped Transformers apply the same layers multiple times per token, adding compute to improve quality without adding parameters. Normally each recursion writes its own key-value (KV) cache, so memory grows with the number of recursions; inference-time tricks can shrink this cache but usually at a quality cost. FineWeb-Edu is a filtered, high-quality educational web dataset commonly used to evaluate language models.

## [SymCE Reveals Imitation Trap in Counterexample Generation for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02444) ⭐️ 8.0/10

The paper introduces SymCE, a corpus of 4,707 false undergraduate-algebra and real-analysis conjectures, each paired with an executable per-theorem Python verifier that also serves as a reward function. Training Qwen3-4B with counterexample-only supervised fine-tuning collapsed true-theorem recognition from 0.27 to 0.00, while reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) using GRPO repaired and exceeded the base model, reaching 0.66. This work exposes a critical failure mode in supervised fine-tuning for mathematical reasoning: training only on counterexamples can destroy a model's ability to recognize true theorems, an 'imitation trap' that replicates across four seeds and on Gemma-3-4B. It shows that RLVR with a sparse outcome-only reward can repair this collapse, offering a more robust training paradigm for formal reasoning and potentially influencing how LLMs are trained for math and verification tasks. The 4B model outperforms every evaluated 7B open-weights math specialist, remains competitive with six frontier commercial APIs, and transfers under unchanged prompting to GSM8K, MATH-500, and MMLU-college-math. A human audit of 177 verifier decisions found 97.7% accuracy, and sparse versus dense rewards were statistically indistinguishable in-domain but diverged by 33 points on a held-out calibration probe, a dissociation traced to the partial-credit term.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Large language models often prove a theorem forward but fail to disprove a closely related false statement, a gap that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) does not close and can worsen. ## [Paper Maps 23 Failure Modes in Compound AI Systems from 150 Incidents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02503) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02503) analyzes 150 production incident reports from open-source compound AI projects and anonymized enterprise deployments to build a taxonomy of 23 failure modes across five categories: retrieval, generation, tool, orchestration, and integration failures. It also proposes resilience patterns validated through controlled fault injection experiments, reporting that circuit breakers cut cascade propagation by 89%, output quality gates catch 73% of silent degradation, and component isolation reduces blast radius by 64%. The taxonomy is organized into five categories (retrieval, generation, tool, orchestration, and integration failures), and the paper reports that systems implementing three or more resilience patterns from the catalog reduce mean-time-to-recovery (MTTR) by 71% versus unstructured monitoring baselines. The incident taxonomy and pattern catalog are released as a public practitioner resource, though the findings are drawn from open-source projects and anonymized enterprise deployments rather than a controlled industry-wide sample.

## [IGNITE: Generative World Model Simulates Tokamak Fusion Plasma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02515) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers introduced IGNITE, a generative world foundation model trained self-supervised on over a decade of unlabeled experimental data from the DIII-D National Fusion Facility. Its auto-regressive dynamics model can simulate entire DIII-D discharges from actuator trajectories, which can be supplied directly or generated on-the-fly from a textual prompt or desired experimental outcomes. This work represents a significant technical advance in AI for scientific simulation, potentially enabling efficient AI-driven experimental planning and plasma control for nuclear fusion. If validated, such world models could reduce the need for costly and time-consuming physical experiments on tokamaks like DIII-D and inform the design and operation of future devices such as ITER. IGNITE uses several spatio-temporal tokenizers to embed different input modalities, including time-series measurement data, image sequences, and high-resolution spectrograms collected at vastly different time scales. Its auto-regressive backbone can predict entire discharges over a theoretical infinite horizon given initial latent plasma states and actuator trajectories, though the abstract does not report quantitative validation metrics.

**Background**: DIII-D is a tokamak operated by General Atomics in San Diego since the late 1980s for the U.S. Department of Energy, and its D-shaped plasma cross-section has become a standard for modern advanced tokamak designs. Tokamaks confine hot plasma with magnetic fields to achieve fusion, but simulating and controlling plasma discharges is extremely challenging due to complex, multi-scale physics. World models are generative models that learn a compressed representation of an environment's dynamics and can roll it forward to predict future states, an approach popularized in AI for video and robotics and now being applied to scientific domains.

## [WebUIProof benchmarks WebUI code generators via UI-agent execution tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02617) ⭐️ 8.0/10

WebUIProof is a new execution-oriented benchmark that evaluates WebUI code generation using structured specifications and dense, executable interaction tests across two task families: general WebUIs (dashboards, games, interactive tools) and 3D interactive simulations (particle/galaxy systems, physics dynamics). Its UI-agent harness runs a plan-act-observe loop in a headless browser, locating DOM elements, performing actions, observing UI/DOM changes, and checking assertions; across eight commercial LLMs, frequent failures occur on interaction-based requirements even when pages render successfully, especially on 3D simulation interfaces. This benchmark addresses a critical gap in evaluating functional correctness of generated WebUI code, since prior benchmarks relied on free-form prompts and static checks like build success or screenshots that miss interaction failures. It could significantly improve how code generators are assessed and, as shown in the paper, the harness can also supply outcome-level training signals that improve compact models. The harness uses an iterative plan-act-observe loop in a headless browser to locate DOM elements, perform actions, observe resulting UI/DOM changes, and verify specified assertions. Training compact models such as Qwen2.5 14B and MIMO 7B with RL rewards derived from these executable interaction tests improves functional completion while reducing build failures.

## [Sigma: First Large-Scale Continuous Diffusion Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02665) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers introduce Sigma, the first large-scale (3B/8B) continuous diffusion language model, built on steerable low-dimensional ODE/SDE latent trajectories and trained blockwise via likelihood optimization. It achieves competitive performance with discrete diffusion and autoregressive baselines on math reasoning and coding benchmarks such as GSM8K, Minerva, HumanEval, MBPP, MATH-500, and AIME. This work shows that continuous diffusion language models can match discrete diffusion and autoregressive models at scale, offering a new paradigm for efficient language generation with steerable trajectories. It could impact reasoning tasks and inference acceleration, where discrete diffusion models struggle due to non-smooth, high-dimensional spaces. Sigma jointly denoises Gaussian-corrupted token embeddings while learning an optimal embedding geometry, and leverages pre-trained autoregressive weights for warm-starting to accelerate training. During inference, classifier-free guidance and score temperature are identified as essential for high-fidelity reasoning and coding, and continuous trajectories enable graceful degradation for low NFEs and efficient distillation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Diffusion models have become dominant in image and video generation, but applying them to language is challenging because text is discrete and categorical, which is incompatible with Gaussian noise corruption. Discrete diffusion language models (dLMs) enable fast parallel decoding but operate in non-smooth, high-dimensional spaces that hinder trajectory steering. Continuous diffusion language models instead map tokens to continuous embeddings, allowing smoother latent trajectories that can be steered for reasoning and inference acceleration.

## [VLMs Can Be Fooled in Training Loss but Not in Free Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03445) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper identifies and mechanistically explains a "train/inference gap" in vision-language models: a targeted PGD adversarial perturbation can drive Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct's teacher-forced training loss for a fixed target caption to near zero, yet the same model, when allowed to generate freely, still produces the original correct description. Using logit lens analysis on 200 held-out COCO images, the authors localize the effect to a single autoregressive step where the target token's rank is fixed at exactly 3,488 out of 152,064 vocabulary entries with zero variance. The findings suggest that adversarial robustness in autoregressive VLMs is substantially a property of the language decoder's prior rather than the visual encoder, which has direct implications for where faithfulness evaluations and defenses for deployed multimodal systems should be targeted. This challenges the common assumption that visual encoders are the primary locus of adversarial vulnerability in VLMs. The study shows that image-level pixel statistics, including a re-implemented texture-based attackability measure from CNN robustness literature, have essentially no predictive power over which images are corrupted (best predictor r=-0.050, p=0.484; ridge regression R^2=0.069). Tracking target-token rank across all 28 LLM decoder layers reveals that the visual encoder corrupts every image's representation by a comparable margin, but the decoder then differentially arbitrates—amplifying the corrupted signal for susceptible images and actively suppressing it past its clean-image baseline for resistant ones (p<0.001, rank-biserial r=0.579); a linear probe on the merger hidden state separates outcomes with AUC=0.858, though the authors flag a circularity concern.

Teacher forcing is a standard training strategy where the model is fed ground-truth previous tokens rather than its own generated outputs, and PGD (projected gradient descent) is a widely used iterative method for crafting adversarial perturbations. The logit lens is a mechanistic interpretability technique that applies a transformer's final unembedding matrix to intermediate residual stream activations to decode next-token predictions at any layer.

A new arXiv paper (2610.03502) introduces a method that formally certifies the behavioral effect of mechanistic edits—ablations, weight edits, and activation steering—proving that disabling a circuit removes one skill while preserving another for every input in a continuous region. EyeRobot 2.0 introduces Active Visual Fixation (AVF), a framework that physically swivels two eye viewpoints to center on a 3D fixation point, enabling fine-grained bimanual manipulation with only a single stereo camera. It uses hierarchical reinforcement learning to train a low-level gaze servoing policy and a target selector, and canonicalizes gripper actions into a fixation-relative SE(3) frame to compact the action distribution. It could significantly impact robotics and embodied AI by enabling precise bimanual tasks with a simpler, single stereo camera setup. In over 1000 physical and 1800 simulated trials, EyeRobot 2.0 outperformed passive stereo by 40% in real and 20% in simulation, matched ego + wrist policies when wrist views were clear (69% vs. 64%), and more than doubled their success when wrist cameras were occluded (48% vs. 22%). The system was trained on teleoperation data from 7 real-world and 6 simulated tasks.

## [ASH: Self-Improving Agents Master Multi-Hour Game Planning from Internet Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14211) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers introduced ASH, an agentic system that learns long-horizon visuomotor policies from unlabeled, noisy internet video without reward shaping or expert action annotations. Using a self-improvement loop that trains an Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM) on its own trajectories to extract supervision from relevant videos, ASH sustained progression across an 8-hour evaluation, reaching 11.2/12 milestones in Pokemon Emerald and 9.9/12 in The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap, outperforming the strongest baselines (9.3/12 and 7.8/12). This work addresses a fundamental bottleneck in AI: scaling long-horizon visuomotor learning without hand-engineered rewards or expensive action-labeled demonstrations. If self-improving agents can reliably extract supervision from raw internet video, it could unlock scalable training for robotics, game-playing, and other sequential decision-making domains where labeled data is scarce. ASH combines unsupervised key-moment identification from large-scale internet video, retained as long-term memory, with an IDM trained on its own trajectories to label video data. It was evaluated on two complementary multi-hour environments—Pokemon Emerald (turn-based RPG) and The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap (real-time action-adventure)—where behavioral cloning, retrieval-augmented, and zero-shot foundation-model baselines all plateaued.

Across 12 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, average success rises from 33.8% to 65.7%, and across four real-robot tasks from 51.4% to 64.6%. With Student histories held fixed, joint video-action supervision achieves the highest observed success on all three ablation tasks, while either modality alone also improves performance; a separate comparison with Teacher-generated histories finds task-dependent differences between the two history sources.

## [ERR-ES Law Formalizes Recovery in Tool-Augmented AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22352) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2601.22352v2) introduces Expected Recovery Regret (ERR), a formal measure of how far a recovery policy deviates from optimal under stochastic execution noise, and derives a first-order law linking ERR to an observable Efficiency Score (ES). The authors empirically validate this ERR-ES law across five tool-use benchmarks spanning controlled perturbations, diagnostic reasoning, and real-world APIs, with predicted regret matching Monte Carlo rollout measurements within delta ≤ 0.05. This work reframes recoverability as a governed property of interaction dynamics rather than an artifact of model scale or architecture, offering a falsifiable theoretical foundation for execution-level robustness in language agents. If the law generalizes, it could give agent developers a measurable design target for building more reliable tool-using systems. The Efficiency Score (ES) is computed from a fixed definition and serves as an observable coordinate on the manifold rather than a fitted objective, so the ERR-ES law should be read as a governed regularity, not a universal identity. Validation covered multiple model scales, perturbation regimes, and recovery horizons, though the paper remains a preprint without peer review.

Expected Recovery Regret (ERR) borrows the concept of regret from online learning and decision theory, measuring the gap between a stochastic recovery policy and the best possible policy under noise. A new arXiv paper (2603.11413v4) challenges a high-profile Nature Medicine study that reported ChatGPT Health under-triages 51.6% of emergencies, arguing the headline rate is largely an artifact of an exam-style scaffold (forced A/B/C/D output, knowledge suppression, no clarifying questions). In a mechanistic study, five frontier LLMs scored 6.4 points higher on naturalistic patient-style messages than under the constrained scaffold (p=0.015), with one vignette jumping from 0-24% under forced choice to 100% with free text; a faithful replication of the authors' own 60 vignettes across six frontier models and four matched formats, with clinician validation, found the direction reversed and showed that every free-text "under-triage" was actually a same-day recommendation scored C rather than D. If headline triage failure rates are largely a property of output format and of mapping prose onto a four-point scale, then safety claims based on exam-style scaffolds may be misleading and could distort policy and deployment decisions. The replication found that free-text rewrites scored slightly below the exact structured prompt (78.7% vs 81.8%, p=0.020), removing only the answer scaffold changed little (80.6% vs 81.4%, p=0.81), and naturalistic input with a forced categorical answer beat both the exact prompt (84.4%, p=0.023) and free text (p=0.0001); on the four vignettes defining the original emergency rate, under-triage was 17% with the exact scaffold, 50% in free text, and 21% with a forced letter, and 60% of free-text cases made escalation conditional on information the patient was asked to check, behavior a single-turn benchmark cannot score.

Deployed on two scientific benchmarks, it identified 12 author-confirmed issues in ScienceAgentBench and exactly matched 83.3% of expert-identified issues on the BIXBench Verified-50 subset. ## [RAO Trains Recursive Agents to Delegate Sub-Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06639) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new paper introduces Recursive Agent Optimization (RAO), a reinforcement learning approach that trains recursive agents — agents that can spawn and delegate sub-tasks to new instantiations of themselves — to decide when and how to delegate and communicate. The authors report that RAO-trained agents achieve better training efficiency, scale to tasks beyond the model's context window, generalize to much harder problems, and reduce wall-clock time versus single-agent systems. This work connects reinforcement learning with inference-time scaling for agents, offering a principled way to train models to exploit divide-and-conquer at test time. It could influence how multi-agent and recursive agent systems are built, especially for long-context and hard reasoning tasks. RAO trains a single LLM policy that is reused at every node of the recursive execution tree, from the root task down to the smallest sub-task, and recursive agents solve tasks whose inputs exceed the model's training context by chunking and delegating to sub-agents. The abstract does not specify model sizes, benchmarks, or exact performance numbers.

A large-scale longitudinal study of 55,393 trending queries over 40 days (March 13 – April 21, 2026) found that Google AI Overviews activate for 13.7% of queries overall and 64.7% of question-form queries, with markedly lower rates on politically sensitive topics. ## [Quantum World Models Beat Classical Finite Memory in Policy Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19779) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.19779v2) proves that classical world models with finite memory cannot always align the optimal policies of real and virtual worlds, even when the true world is classical. The authors construct true worlds where every finite classical model fails along the same trajectory, while a quantum world model using a single qutrit reproduces the world exactly and keeps optimal policies perfectly aligned. This establishes an irreducible quantum advantage for world-model alignment, with direct implications for AI safety, reinforcement learning, and quantum machine learning. It suggests that for certain long-horizon environments, no amount of classical memory suffices, and quantum resources may be fundamentally necessary to keep simulated policies faithful to reality. The failure mode is specific: every finite classical model either loses the ability to distinguish actions when the true world clearly prefers one, or repeatedly assigns the highest expected reward to suboptimal actions, and its expected-reward estimates retain a nonvanishing average error. In contrast, the single-qutrit quantum model's reward estimates and preferred actions always match the true world, guaranteeing policy alignment.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: World models are learned simulators that predict the next observation and reward given an action, letting reinforcement learning agents be trained and tested before costly real-world deployment. When present outcomes depend on events far in the past, the model needs memory to capture those long-range dependencies. A qutrit is a three-level quantum system, the quantum analogue of a classical bit or qubit, and here it serves as the minimal quantum memory resource. AI alignment concerns ensuring that a model's learned objective and resulting policy match what we actually intend.

## [Screw Attention Embeds Rigid-Body Algebra into Transformer Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00904) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Screw Attention, a transformer layer that represents inter-token relations as spatial transforms (relative poses and joint screws) rather than graph edges. A 16k-parameter policy trained only from object poses achieves 97.3% success on the LIBERO-Spatial benchmark, outperforming graph, transformer, and flat networks of the same size as well as a flat network with 27 times more parameters. This work bridges robotics, geometric deep learning, and transformer architectures by embedding a principled inductive bias—rigid-body mechanics—directly into attention, potentially enabling far more sample-efficient and robust manipulation policies. The equivariance property makes policies robust to changes in frame conventions, addressing a key fragility of learned manipulation policies. Messages are transported along the relation into the receiver's frame, while attention scores see only frame-invariant quantities, making messages equivariant to independent frame changes at every token. Ablations show the gain comes from transporting correct relations, and the policy tolerates pose noise and calibration errors at least as well as an analytic controller; used as a gated residual on an analytic controller, it also improves a contact-rich insertion task.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Screw theory is a mathematical framework in robotics that represents rigid-body motions and forces as pairs of vectors (twists and wrenches), providing closed-form descriptions of spatial relations. Transformers are neural network architectures that use attention to model relationships between tokens, but standard attention treats relations as graph edges without geometric structure. LIBERO-Spatial is a benchmark suite for evaluating spatial-relation manipulation tasks in lifelong robot learning, where policies must generalize across spatial configurations.

## [Fold'EM infers atomic structures directly from cryo-EM particles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01358) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Fold'EM is an inference-time framework that combines priors from protein generative models directly with cryo-EM particle images to determine atomic models from a small number of single-particle images, bypassing both intermediate density reconstruction and downstream model building. Across synthetic and experimental datasets, it recovers accurate atomic structures with known particle orientations and in an ab-initio setting where orientations are inferred jointly with structure, and it resolves distinct conformational states from mixed particle populations without separately reconstructing a density map for each state. This could significantly improve throughput and reduce sample requirements for cryo-EM structure determination, especially for heterogeneous samples where conventional density reconstruction has high sample complexity. It opens new avenues for characterizing low-population conformational states directly from particles, which is important for structural biology and drug discovery. The method works both with known particle orientations and in an ab-initio setting where orientations are inferred jointly with structure, and it handles heterogeneous datasets by resolving distinct conformational states from mixed populations without reconstructing a separate density map for each state. The abstract does not specify the exact number of particles required or the resolution limits achieved.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is a widely used technique for determining biomolecular structures. The conventional computational pipeline first combines many particle images to reconstruct an electrostatic potential (ESP) map, then fits an atomic model to that map; this density reconstruction step requires large numbers of particle images and becomes difficult for heterogeneous samples and low-resolution maps. Protein structure prediction models provide strong sequence-derived priors on atomic structure, but in cryo-EM these priors are typically integrated only after density reconstruction during atomic model fitting.

A new arXiv paper presents a paired, self-audited evaluation of an open-weight System-1 decision model (Laya) and a hosted one (Jev) across 11 agent decision points built from 18 public sources, using 7,283 base cases plus 6,640 robustness variants with byte-identical inputs. Jev was significantly more accurate on 9 of 11 decision points (+10.8 to +46.0 percentage points), but neither model beat chance on zero-shot model routing, and Laya flipped 30% of its answers when option order was reversed. This study gives agent builders concrete evidence about when cheap System-1 decision models can replace full LLM calls and when they cannot, showing that routing and RAG relevance gating remain unreliable. It also demonstrates a self-auditing methodology that caught errors inflating deployment claims, which could raise the bar for how agent evaluation papers report results. Laya degraded sharply with many or similar candidates, dropping to 31% accuracy at 50 nearest-neighbour tools versus 98% for Jev on items with a unique correct tool. The authors' self-audit found three analysis errors and one design confound: an omitted pre-screen cost (reported 23.9% saving, actual 4.3%), gate accuracy misreported as end-to-end quality (58% vs. 98%), in-sample thresholds (5% target, up to 17% held-out misses), and a channel effect on injection false positives that vanished with channel-native content.

## [LLM Analysis of 9,821 UK Annual Reports Reveals AI Risk Disclosure Surge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02281) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper applies a reproducible two-stage LLM classification pipeline to 9,821 annual reports from 1,362 UK listed companies (2020-2025), finding that AI risk mentions rose from 2.8% to 41.2% and AI adoption disclosures from 13.8% to 45.2%. The study also introduces a substantiveness classification showing that in 2025 only 4.3% of reports contained substantive AI risk disclosure despite 41.2% mentioning AI as a risk. This work demonstrates that LLM-processed annual reports can serve as a scalable, actionable signal for AI governance and societal resilience research, giving policymakers and researchers a new empirical lens on corporate AI behavior. The stark gap between nominal and substantive disclosure suggests current corporate AI risk reporting may be largely performative, with important implications for regulators relying on such disclosures. The pipeline was validated against 474 human-annotated passages, achieving high recall but only moderate label-level agreement, and the analysis covers partial 2026 data. Disclosure varies by sector and market segment: AIM reports disclose AI risk at far lower rates than Main Market reports, Energy and Data Infrastructure sectors lag behind, and harm disclosures are nearly absent with only seven reports across the entire corpus.

## [CALM: Prompt-Local Counterfactual Correction for Safer Text-to-Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02300) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02300) analyzes the limits of the "global unsafety" assumption in text-to-image safety filters and proposes CALM (Counterfactual Adaptive Local Modulation), a training-free safeguard that replaces uniform global removal with prompt-local counterfactual correction. Using matched unsafe-benign anchors, CALM routes each prompt to active unsafe categories, minimally edits only violating token representations, and suppresses positively aligned unsafe residual components. The work identifies a consistent coverage-selectivity trade-off in existing global safety filters: compact unsafe subspaces fail to cover heterogeneous unsafe semantics, while broader aggregation increasingly distorts safety-adjacent benign prompts. CALM demonstrates that local counterfactual correction can significantly improve unsafe content suppression while preserving benign utility, offering a practical alternative to blunt global signal removal for AI safety in generative models. CALM is training-free and operates by routing prompts to active unsafe categories via matched unsafe-benign anchors, then minimally editing only violating token representations toward the safe side while suppressing positively aligned unsafe residual components. The paper reports broad evaluation showing improved unsafe content suppression with preserved benign utility, though the abstract does not specify exact benchmarks, model architectures, or quantitative metrics.

## [SatisDive Balances Reward and Diversity in Text-to-Image Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02372) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper formulates text-to-image generation as a satisficing problem where every image must meet a reward floor and the batch must meet a diversity cutoff, and introduces SatisDive, a training-free inference-time method that traverses the resulting Pareto frontier. On Pick-a-Pic at matched DreamSim, SatisDive improves worst-candidate reward over FK steering by up to 0.43 with FLUX.1-dev and HPSv3, and by up to 0.70 with SANA-1.6B and ImageReward. Existing approaches either handle reward and diversity separately or merge them into one aggregate score, which lets high diversity mask low rewards; by enforcing a reward floor and diversity cutoff, this work offers a principled way to control the trade-off. It matters for controllable generative AI, where users want multiple prompt images that are both high-quality and visually distinct. SatisDive uses a batch-relative reward cutoff to separate lower- from higher-reward candidates, emphasizing reward improvement below the cutoff and diversity above it, and it is training-free, operating purely at inference time. Across overlapping DreamSim ranges, its satisfaction-diversity curve Pareto-dominates FK steering's curve in each tested setting.

**Background**: Text-to-image diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising in a compressed latent space, and users often sample several images from the same prompt. A learned reward model scores how well an image matches user preferences, while diversity measures how visually different the images are from one another. Satisficing is a decision strategy that accepts any option meeting an acceptability threshold rather than optimizing a single objective, and a Pareto frontier describes the set of solutions where no objective can be improved without worsening another.

## [FlashSinkhorn 2: Two-Stage GPU Solver for Large-Scale Entropic Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02395) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FlashSinkhorn 2 (FS2) is a new two-stage GPU solver for entropic optimal transport (EOT) on low-dimensional point clouds with squared-Euclidean cost. It combines a coarse stage that solves on cell centroids and lifts potentials to all points with a block-sparse fine stage that corrects residual centroid error, achieving a prescribed marginal residual on all 32 synthetic benchmarks and solving a 1.34×10^8-particle cosmological EOT problem on a single A100 in under 2.5 hours. This work pushes the boundary of what size of discrete EOT problem can be solved to high accuracy on a single GPU, which matters for researchers and practitioners in large-scale optimal transport, GPU-accelerated optimization, and scientific computing. By avoiding the dense n×m kernel evaluation in every Sinkhorn iteration, FS2 makes previously intractable problems—such as cosmological N-body transport—feasible within hours. FS2 uses Morton-ordered blocks to support screening and fused tensor-core execution, with a threshold set by block masses that bounds each omitted tile's contribution to every row and column. The coarse stage continues on centroids when a sampled marginal check rejects the lift, replacing most point-level updates, while the fine stage removes the centroid error that coarse updates cannot.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Entropic optimal transport (EOT) adds an entropy regularization term to the classical optimal transport problem, making it solvable by the Sinkhorn algorithm, which iteratively scales a cost matrix to satisfy marginal constraints. The Sinkhorn algorithm traditionally requires evaluating all n×m point pairs per iteration, which becomes prohibitive for very large point clouds. FlashSinkhorn introduced a streaming GPU approach that avoids storing the dense kernel, and FlashSinkhorn 2 extends this with a two-stage coarse-to-fine strategy.

## [Tropical RL Replaces Expected Return with Max for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02478) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.02478) proposes Tropical Reinforcement Learning, which swaps the standard sum of probabilities over successful trajectories for a max operation drawn from the tropical semiring. The authors introduce TROPIC, a training algorithm for deterministic, resettable environments with verifiable outcomes, and report gains of up to 16 percentage points over the strongest on-policy baselines on Sokoban, Countdown, FrozenLake, and WebShop. Expected return only measures how often a policy succeeds, not which solution worked, and because probabilities sum to one, reinforcing one solution can cause the model to forget another valid one. Changing the underlying algebra rather than just the estimator could substantially improve compositional reasoning in LLMs, with potential implications for RLHF and agentic reasoning research. Under the tropical semiring, the value of a state becomes the log-probability of its most likely verified solution, along with an explicit replayable path, so the best prefix and best suffix meeting at a shared state can be joined even when they originate from different rollouts. The approach is limited to deterministic, resettable environments with verifiable outcomes, and the paper is a preprint with no community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: The tropical semiring is an algebraic structure in which the usual addition and multiplication are replaced by max (or min) and addition respectively; it underlies tropical geometry and is named after Brazilian-based computer scientist Imre Simon. Reinforcement learning for LLMs typically maximizes expected return by summing the probabilities of all successful trajectories, which works well for measuring success frequency but struggles when a correct answer must be assembled from reasoning steps that appear only across separate, often failed attempts.

## [Typed Decision Models Rely on Option Labels, Not Definitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02586) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02586) shows that open-weight typed decision models — systems that return a probability for each caller-defined option — largely base their answers on option labels rather than the written definitions. Across four models, three answer-reading methods on a Qwen2.5 backbone, eleven classification tasks, and a new synthetic routing suite called PolicyBench, deleting all definitions left accuracy essentially unchanged (laya-td: 0.8559 vs 0.8487), while renaming options to 'A' and 'B' raised accuracy by +0.1511. This exposes a critical flaw in a common interface used for routing, moderation, and triage, meaning developers who write careful rules in option definitions may be getting decisions driven by superficial label strings instead. The authors trace the cause to prompt rendering rather than the constrained decision head, and provide a two-call test plus mitigation measurements, which is directly actionable for anyone using LLMs as classifiers or decision-makers. The effect appears to stem from one expression in the prompt rendering: laya writes each option as "{label}: {definition}", while von writes only the definition. Changing that expression in both directions with no weight changes made all three laya checkpoints exactly invariant (+0.0000) and created the effect in von, whose accuracy fell from 0.8511 to 0.2281 when a label contradicted its definition; definitions alone still supported 0.7971 accuracy.

## [Email Agents Fail When Requests Are Phrased Indirectly or Formally](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02627) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02627) constructs validated request variants along five communication-style axes and four rule-based dialect conditions, then evaluates them on three benchmarks: one retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and two tool-using agents. It finds that indirect requests reduce performance on all three benchmarks, while formal requests reduce performance on both agentic benchmarks. The results show that a successful response is not enough to establish robustness, since assistants can silently do less work when the same request is phrased differently. This matters for anyone deploying email assistants or other tool-using agents, because current benchmarks that test only one canonical request may overstate real-world reliability. The failures have different causes: verbose requests mainly hurt a lexical retriever by making the relevant email harder to find, whereas indirect and dialect variants remain harmful even when the relevant email is retrieved. In the agentic setting, indirect and formal requests mainly cause agents to omit required actions rather than take more unsupported actions.

Tool-using agents are AI systems that augment language models with access to external operations such as search engines, APIs, or databases, allowing them to take structured actions. A lexical retriever is a search component that matches documents based on exact terms or words, such as BM25, rather than on semantic meaning.

## [DuplexJev: Frozen LLM Answers Speech Decisions Without Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose DuplexJev, which feeds ASR-encoder hidden states through a small connector into a frozen LLM and reads each closed question as a single-token distribution over its options, avoiding autoregressive decoding entirely. An 8-GPU node answers 80 decisions about eight utterances in about 0.1 seconds, and with a cross-attention connector, gender and emotion recognition both reach 90% accuracy (up from 55% and 28%). Full-duplex voice agents must make many small, closed decisions in real time, and slow autoregressive decoding is a major bottleneck; this single-token supervision approach enables fast batched inference while also improving paralinguistic accuracy. It could significantly impact the design of real-time speech systems and multimodal agents that need to perceive speaker attributes beyond the transcript. With a last-layer connector, spoken QA stays close to reading the transcript (90% vs. 91%), while the cross-attention connector trades only 1 point of spoken QA (83% to 82%) for large gains in speaker attributes. Decisions are trained with cross-entropy on the read-out answer token rather than the usual transcript distillation, whose teacher never hears the voice, and distillation is kept only for content; encoders and LLMs are interchangeable, and weights, training recipe, a batched-inference pipeline, and a bilingual spoken-QA set are released.

**Background**: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) encoders convert audio into hidden states, which are typically decoded into text by a decoder. Large language models (LLMs) can be frozen and reused as fixed feature processors, and knowledge distillation is a common technique for transferring behavior from a stronger teacher model to a smaller student. ## [SR-OPD Cuts On-Policy Distillation Teacher Tokens to 3.46-5.02%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02678) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02678) introduces Success-Referenced On-Policy Distillation (SR-OPD), which selectively applies teacher supervision only to failed student rollouts that diverge from a successful reference rollout for the same prompt. Across three teacher-student pairs and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SR-OPD uses just 3.46-5.02% of the teacher-input tokens required by Vanilla OPD in the one-pass setting while maintaining comparable reasoning performance. On-policy distillation normally requires the teacher to grade every token of every student rollout, which is computationally expensive and a major bottleneck for scaling distillation pipelines. SR-OPD shows that a student's own successful behavior can serve as a reference for allocating teacher supervision under a fixed budget, potentially making distillation far cheaper for teams training smaller reasoning models. SR-OPD focuses on prompts where the student produces both successful and failed rollouts, and prioritizes failed rollouts whose hidden-state trajectories show sustained divergence from a successful reference, while also accounting for estimated teacher-input cost. Controlled experiments matched to 5% of Vanilla OPD's teacher-input budget support both key design choices: focusing on prompts with mixed success/failure and using successful rollouts to guide failure selection.

**Background**: Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller student model, and on-policy distillation (OPD) refines the student using dense token-level supervision on trajectories the student itself generates, which helps address exposure bias. However, providing teacher supervision for every rollout is costly, so methods that selectively allocate teacher computation are of growing interest. ## [LLMs Update Clinical Judgment Unreliably as Patient Evidence Evolves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02684) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.02684) evaluates longitudinal belief updating in large language models using matched intensive-care trajectories from electronic health records, finding that conditioning on a preceding judgment more often increased than reduced prediction error when estimates changed. Controlled interventions revealed two failure modes: models responded more strongly to worsening than to matched improving respiratory evidence, and raising prior risk from 10% to 90% shifted estimates by 26.2 percentage points, showing a causal influence of prior model beliefs. This work establishes longitudinal belief updating as a distinct dimension of LLM reliability, which matters for AI safety and clinical decision support because models that fail to revise judgments appropriately as new patient data arrives could mislead clinicians. The findings suggest that current prompting strategies cannot fix these failures, so developers of medical AI systems may need new training or architectural approaches before deploying LLMs in evolving clinical settings. The asymmetry between worsening and improving evidence persisted after headroom normalization at moderate and strong evidence levels, and the paper introduces Evidence-Validated Longitudinal Update (EVLU), which identified fewer but more reliable revisions, revealing a reliability-coverage trade-off. The study is a preprint based on retrospective EHR data rather than prospective clinical trials, and prompting alone did not restore reliable updating.

For each query, GraphMemory retrieves only the relevant subgraph, achieving competitive downstream performance while using approximately 81-85% fewer memory-construction tokens than baselines. This work addresses a critical bottleneck in LLM agent memory: continually appending information to a shared context causes token costs to grow, hits context-window limits, and degrades performance. By decoupling memory from context and keeping retrieved memory constant under bounded retrieval, it offers a principled path toward scalable test-time continual learning for enterprise, scientific, and medical agents. The paper frames an agent memory system update as an optimization update procedure over the model's context, providing a theoretical lens for studying memory design efficiency. Under bounded retrieval, the amount of retrieved memory remains constant as the number of processed examples grows; the largest token reduction occurs on Formula with Claude Haiku 4.5, where GraphMemory uses roughly 20M training tokens versus 131M for the ACE baseline.

BitNest introduces a bit-nested speculative decoding framework that embeds a low-precision draft directly into the higher-precision target representation, so both models share a single physical weight representation. Across multiple 7B–8B edge-friendly LLMs, it achieves an average speculative acceptance rate of 95.2% and 1.48–1.61x end-to-end speedup over FP16 autoregressive decoding. Rather than deriving a draft from a predefined target, BitNest first builds a strong low-precision base and then recovers the higher-precision target through residual refinement, and it extends this progressive-precision design to the KV cache for long-context inference. On LLaMA models supported by all representative self-speculative baselines, it achieves competitive or higher decoding speedup.

Quantization compresses model weights into lower-precision formats such as 8-bit or 4-bit integers to reduce memory and compute, while the KV cache stores per-head key and value states so transformers do not recompute attention over the whole context for every new token. BitNest combines these ideas by nesting a quantized draft inside the full-precision target weights.

By compressing the cache online without irreversibly deleting historical states, iS-KV offers a practical path to serving long-horizon reasoning models more efficiently, which matters to researchers and practitioners working on efficient LLM inference. The core insight is that updating the low-rank basis for new tokens while old tokens keep coordinates in the old basis causes substantial drift in stored history; iS-KV therefore synchronizes historical coordinates with the evolving basis to maintain representation consistency. It keeps a recent window exact and incrementally folds older states into bounded-rank representations, achieving persistent-KV compression of 4.06x and 5.64x on the two tested models.

SVD-based low-rank compression is an alternative that retains all positions in a more compact form, but extending it from a fixed prompt cache to online decoding is non-trivial because the low-rank basis must evolve as new tokens arrive.
