## [MetaRubric Fixes Vacuous Credit in Rubric-Based RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02824) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.02824) introduces MetaRubric, a method that alternates evidence-aware policy optimization with response-guided rubric adaptation to eliminate a failure mode called Vacuous Credit, where rubric judges award high criterion scores even when the required information is absent from a response. Using counterfactual prompts that change one task-relevant fact, MetaRubric improves PubMedQA accuracy by 6.00–20.40 percentage points over static-judge GRPO across multiple backbones, with additional gains on HealthBench-Hard and two multimodal medical benchmarks. This work identifies a previously unnamed failure mode in rubric-based reinforcement learning and offers a concrete counterfactual remedy, which could make reward modeling for open-ended tasks more reliable and improve RLHF pipelines that depend on partial-credit rubrics. The reported gains on medical QA benchmarks suggest the approach may be especially valuable in high-stakes domains where missing evidence should not be rewarded. MetaRubric assigns credit only when a response contains sufficient evidence to satisfy a rubric criterion, and after each policy-optimization stage it uses current policy responses to revise both original and counterfactual criteria while preserving the original prompt's intended meaning. Criterion weights are also adapted at stage boundaries to address observed policy errors, though the work is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community validation yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Rubric-based reinforcement learning extends reward-driven optimization to open-ended tasks by assigning partial credit to individual response requirements, but judges can be fooled into awarding credit for content that is not actually present. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement-learning algorithm for LLMs that samples a group of answers per prompt and uses the group's average reward as a baseline, so spurious credit can reverse the sign of a response's advantage. Counterfactual prompting is a technique that asks a model to consider hypothetical alternatives to actual facts, which MetaRubric uses to construct paired prompts differing by one task-relevant fact.

## [Recursive Self-Rewrite Turns Harness Trajectories into Training Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02826) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint introduces Recursive Self-Rewrite (RSR), a framework where a single base model, Qwen-3.8-27B, discovers successful solutions under diverse harnesses and rewrites them into training trajectories for a general harness. Across roughly 3K self-curated terminal tasks, three harnesses jointly solved 759 tasks (34.3% more than the strongest single harness), and RSR expanded 2,001 source trajectories into 11,094 rewritten trajectories, lifting pass@3 on Terminal-Bench 2 from 57.0% to 74.2% and on Terminal-Bench 4 from 1.5% to 9.1%. This work shows that experiences gathered under specialized, harness-assisted conditions can be reconstructed into reusable capabilities for a model operating under a general harness, addressing a key gap between benchmark performance and real deployment. It offers a practical recipe for scaling self-improvement and agent training data, which could benefit teams building terminal or software agents that must work without bespoke scaffolding. RSR uses a planner to extract procedures into runbooks, a critic to screen for verifier and solution leakage and guide recursive revision, and an executor to follow qualified runbooks in fresh sandboxes. Training on the rewritten trajectories outperforms both the base model and direct trajectory SFT, with process reward on Long-Horizon Terminal-Bench rising from 0.21 to 0.29, though the results are from an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

## [AMBER: Adaptive Budget Allocation for Vision-Language Reranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02831) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AMBER introduces an online, budgeted multi-view reranking framework that dynamically allocates vision-language model (VLM) calls using continuous Elo updates and information-gain-based query scheduling. Experiments on CIRR, CIRCO, and PhotoBench show it achieves the strongest overall performance among compared multi-call VLM reranking methods under comparable VLM-call budgets, with code released at https://github.com/wnlfc/AMBER. VLM-based listwise reranking is powerful but expensive, so AMBER's ability to cut wasted VLM calls could make high-quality multimodal retrieval more practical for real-world systems with tight inference budgets. It also offers a principled bridge between classic rating models and modern efficient inference research. AMBER treats fragmented listwise VLM outputs as local tournaments and maintains a lightweight global ranking state via Elo updates, which the authors show correspond to stochastic gradient ascent steps on the Bradley-Terry log-likelihood. It allocates computation at two levels—constructing candidate views with high score ambiguity and scheduling queries to maximize expected information gain—with a submodular information-theoretic motivation for the query-level strategy.

The Elo rating system, originally designed for chess, is a special case of the Bradley-Terry model and provides a way to maintain relative rankings from pairwise comparison outcomes.

## [SSM Safety Heads Certified Robust via Contraction Condition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02853) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.02853) proves that State Space Model (SSM)-based safety heads can be certified robust against bounded embedding-space perturbations if and only if the l∞ norm of the state transition matrix satisfies ‖A‖∞ < 1, a condition called the contraction condition. Enforcing this with a hinge penalty improved certified fraction on toxic comment data from 41% to 59%, and a contraction-regularized S4 head achieved zero-shot jailbreak detection with DR=0.994 on AdvBench and DR=0.988 on HarmBench. This work provides the first formal robustness certification for SSM-based safety heads, addressing a critical gap in AI safety where empirical detection performance has been studied but formal guarantees were lacking. It could enable provably reliable jailbreak detection and influence how safety classifiers are designed and deployed in high-stakes settings. When the contraction condition holds, the reachable output interval has bounded steady-state width and exact interval bound propagation (IBP) certification is possible; when it fails, the interval grows exponentially with sequence length and certification is impossible at any practical perturbation radius. Notably, a simple logistic regression on mean-pooled Mamba-130M embeddings matches or exceeds the S4 head on every detection metric, confirming harmful intent is already linearly separable and the S4 head's value lies in certification, not superior discrimination.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: State Space Models (SSMs) like S4 and Mamba are sequence modeling architectures that process inputs through a hidden state governed by a state transition matrix A, offering efficient long-context handling. Safety heads are lightweight classifiers attached to pretrained language models to flag harmful inputs before generation, but their formal robustness—guarantees that predictions stay stable under small input perturbations—has been largely unexplored. Interval bound propagation (IBP) is a certified training technique that computes worst-case output bounds over input ranges, and the contraction condition ‖A‖∞ < 1 ensures these bounds remain finite and tight.

Across multiple long-horizon agent benchmarks and models, HAD outperforms on-policy distillation baselines with the same fixed harness, entering fewer unproductive loops and recovering from errors more often.

## [Router-Gradient Sensitivity Beats Activation Frequency for Finding Safety-Critical MoE Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02910) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.02910v1) shows that ranking experts by router-gradient sensitivity — the sensitivity of sequence loss to the gate weights selecting an expert — identifies safety-critical experts in sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs better than the conventional activation-frequency signal. Across five MoE architectures and two suppression budgets (equal expert counts and equal malicious routing traffic of 1%–5%), gradient-based selection reduced refusals more than activation frequency in 24 of 25 conditions, and more than a ten-trial random mean in all 25; in OLMoE, refusals dropped from 34 to 9 out of 100 prompts (73.53% relative) without degraded outputs. This reframes MoE safety as a routing-security problem: if suppressing a small set of experts can silently weaken refusal behavior without retraining, then knowing which experts actually influence safety is critical for red-teaming, model auditing, and deployment safeguards. It also suggests that widely used frequency-based importance metrics may systematically miss the experts that matter most for alignment, affecting how practitioners prune, compress, or monitor MoE models. The study ranks experts on 500 benign and 500 malicious prompts and measures refusal on 100 held-out malicious prompts; even after matching expert counts in every layer, gradient selection still outperformed activation in 23 of 25 conditions with two ties. An exploratory cross-model analysis links larger malicious-versus-benign concentration gaps to greater peak gradient effects (rho = 0.90; exact two-sided p = 0.083, n = 5), a correlation that is suggestive but not statistically significant given the small sample.

Verification works in two ways: masking a selected evidence entry is compared against masking a comparable control entry to test evidence-to-proof grounding, and removing a preference claim is used to measure the drop in the target item's ranking margin to test proof-to-recommendation influence. A ranking-preservation objective keeps useful information from the full history, and the paper reports that PROVE-REC produces claims that are both more strongly grounded and more influential while preserving ranking quality.

## [CISE Uses Conformal Intervals to Make LLM Self-Evolution Reliable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02975) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02975) proposes Conformal Interval-Driven Self-Evolution (CISE), a method that builds candidate-specific reward intervals using conditional conformal inference and iteration-wise online density-ratio estimation. In experiments on three materials-science self-evolving search tasks, all candidates returned by CISE were true positives under high-fidelity evaluation, while baselines returned more candidates but included false positives. This matters because many scientific-discovery domains cannot afford high-fidelity evaluation of every candidate, so self-evolving LLM systems must rely on cheap but imperfect proxy rewards that can reward infeasible candidates. By delivering a smaller, statistically calibrated shortlist, CISE could make LLM-driven discovery more trustworthy when downstream validation budgets are limited. CISE uses conservative interval-based rewards for evolutionary feedback and only returns candidates when all required property intervals lie entirely within their feasible regions. The authors derive fixed-iteration coverage results under explicit assumptions of independence and covariate shift, and the code is available at https://github.com/MLAI-Yonsei/CISE.git.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Conformal inference is a framework for uncertainty quantification that turns point predictions into statistically valid prediction regions with guaranteed coverage. LLM-based self-evolving search lets a model iteratively generate and refine candidates for scientific discovery, but it needs a reward signal to guide each generation. When high-fidelity evaluation is too expensive, systems use proxy rewards, which can suffer from reward hacking — optimizing an imperfect proxy leads to poor true performance. Density-ratio estimation is a technique for comparing two probability distributions without estimating each density separately, often used to correct for covariate shift.

## [RED: Training-Free Decoding Method Mitigates Audio-Visual Hallucinations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02976) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Relevant Evidence Decoding (RED), a training-free method that uses pointwise mutual information (PMI) to identify question-relevant perceptual evidence and selectively strengthen its contribution in Audio-Visual Large Language Models (AV-LLMs). RED decomposes the joint audio-visual contribution into audio, video, and residual interaction components, and a question-only inference pass determines which evidence type to augment. Cross-modal hallucinations remain a critical challenge in AV-LLMs, where one modality can incorrectly influence predictions about another, and RED offers a practical, training-free solution that improves accuracy by up to 7% on CMM, 6.3% on AVHBench, and 3.8% on SVHalluc across three benchmarks and three models. This could inspire further research into evidence-aware decoding strategies for multimodal AI, benefiting applications that rely on robust audio-visual understanding. RED uses pointwise mutual information to quantify the predictive support provided by audio and video beyond the question alone, and it requires an average relative time to first token of 1.5x standard decoding. The method is evaluated on three audio-visual hallucination benchmarks (CMM, AVHBench, SVHalluc) and three AV-LLMs, but the abstract lacks detailed experimental results or community discussion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Audio-Visual Large Language Models (AV-LLMs) process both audio and video inputs to answer questions, but they often suffer from cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality incorrectly affects predictions about another. Contrastive decoding is a common technique to reduce hallucinations in vision-language models by contrasting outputs from different inputs, but its direct extension to AV-LLMs overlooks that different questions require different perceptual evidence. Pointwise mutual information (PMI) is a measure from information theory that quantifies how much one event informs about another, and it has been used in decoding to improve faithfulness in language generation.

## [PLCWorld: A Closed-Loop Benchmark for LLM-Generated PLC Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02982) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced PLCWorld, a closed-loop execution environment and benchmark that couples Structured Text (ST) execution with simulated plant responses and sensor feedback to evaluate LLM-generated PLC programs. It contains 100 synthetic tasks and 473 registered task-condition pairs across Motion Control and Material Handling, and reports Task Success and Safety Violation separately, with direct GPT-5.5 achieving 82.70% Task Success on Easy cases but only 25.10% on Hard cases. This addresses a real gap in evaluating LLM code generation for industrial automation, where correctness must be judged not just by code syntax but by how control commands affect device and workpiece states over time. It provides a shared, reproducible protocol for comparing LLMs and generation-and-verification workflows on both task completion and safety, which matters for anyone deploying AI in safety-critical control systems. Difficulty is defined by control-dependency scope, and validation combines practitioner review, reference and alternative programs, targeted counterexamples, specification-evaluator alignment checks, and comparisons with independent ST runtimes. All 542 targeted counterexamples activate their designated evaluator rules under at least one registered condition, and an "Execution Gap" metric relates submission-profile acceptance to subsequent task failure or observed Safety Violation.

## [DyadMem: A Long-Term Memory Benchmark for How Agents Work with Users](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03020) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced DyadMem, a long-term memory benchmark that jointly annotates user-side memory and a newly defined User-conditioned Relational Agent Memory (URAM) along the same multi-session trajectories. The dataset contains 3,065 episodes, 50,961 sessions, and 61,210 QA instances across 6 memory categories, with session-level Capture and Update gold annotations and two QA settings (Gold-Memory and Full-Pipeline). Existing benchmarks mostly supervise user facts or cross-user reusable experience, leaving relationship-specific agent memory implicit, so DyadMem fills an under-explored gap in evaluating how agents adapt to individual users over time. Its finding that Full-Pipeline QA drops sharply compared with Gold-Memory QA across 20 models suggests current memory pipelines are far from reliable in real multi-session use. Across 16 open-weight and 4 proprietary models, Gold-Memory QA is consistently strong while Full-Pipeline QA drops sharply, and quantitative results reveal low Capture recall, incomplete Recall, and unsafe-deletion issues even in frontier LLMs. A separate experiment validates that URAM yields positive effects for all 20 models, though the work is a benchmark and dataset contribution rather than a new model architecture.

## [Numerical Signals Unpredictably Shift LLM Cooperation in Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03033) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.03033) tests four popular LLMs playing four strategic games with different cooperation equilibria, comparing how natural language, numerical signals, and random sequences affect cooperation levels. It finds that structured messages alter final payoffs for most games and models, but without any predictable pattern, and that agent-generated numerical messages deviate from randomness in ways tied to the payoff structure. The results challenge the common assumption that LLM-based agents converge to stable equilibria regardless of added communication capabilities, which matters for AI safety and multi-agent system design. The authors argue that monitoring AI coordination through restricted channels should prioritize message-level fingerprints, which generalize across models, over behavioral decisions, which do not. The study covers four LLMs and four games with distinct cooperation equilibria, and also varies the agents' assigned personalities. Agent-generated numerical messages become more concentrated with repetition and are mostly associated with the payoff structure, yet remain difficult for humans to interpret, adding an interpretability challenge.

## [Persuasion Between AI Agents Defies Model Scale Predictions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03095) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.03095) measures persuasion as the probabilistic shift in an agent's decision after a single exchange with a dissenting peer, testing seven open-weight language models across three language understanding tasks. It finds that persuasion is strong, and that neither standalone certainty nor model scale reliably predicts which agents will be persuaded or how persuasive they are. As multi-agent systems increasingly mix language models of different families and sizes, this finding suggests that the behavior of interacting models cannot be inferred from their individual properties, which has direct implications for AI safety, reliability, and the design of agent pipelines. The study shows that the size of the decision shift depends more on the susceptibility of the listener than on the persuasiveness of the speaker, and that persuasion patterns are specific to each model pairing, with heterogeneity amplifying persuasion in some combinations and suppressing it in others. Notably, a dissenting agent running a small model can overturn the judgments of a much larger one.

## [LSCO Uses mRNA Language Model Latent Space for Codon Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03098) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Latent-Space Codon Optimization (LSCO), which recasts discrete codon optimization as continuous latent space search using a pretrained mRNA language model, enabling gradient-based optimization. On a real-world wet-lab antibody expression dataset, LSCO outperformed frequency-based and modern deep generative baselines in predicted expression while retaining suitable biophysical properties. Codon optimization is central to therapeutic protein production and mRNA vaccines, but its discrete, combinatorially large design space has long precluded gradient-based methods. By enabling efficient gradient-based search with a data-driven expression objective, LSCO could improve protein yields and accelerate development in biopharmaceutical and mRNA therapeutic pipelines. LSCO combines four components: a data-driven expression objective from an uncertainty-aware predictor, a Minimum-Free-Energy regularizer for structural stability, a naturalness prior from a protein-to-codon back-translation model, and constrained decoding for protein fidelity. The approach was validated on a real-world wet-lab antibody expression dataset, though results are based on predicted expression rather than direct experimental measurements.

**Background**: Codon optimization is the process of selecting synonymous codons—different triplets of nucleotides that encode the same amino acid—to improve mRNA translation efficiency and protein expression. Because the genetic code is degenerate, with 64 codons encoding only 20 amino acids, there are many possible sequences for the same protein, and the design space is discrete and combinatorially large. Existing tools often rely on heuristic proxies such as the Codon Adaptation Index or GC-content, which poorly capture true expression. mRNA language models are pretrained neural networks that learn patterns from large mRNA sequence datasets, and their latent spaces can provide a continuous representation of sequences.

## [TradeGrad Uses Textual Gradients to Optimize Trading Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03128) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces TradeGrad, an experience-guided textual-gradient framework that optimizes quantitative trading strategies by having an LLM iteratively rewrite strategy source code based on backtest feedback. It adds a Cross-Period Robust Objective (CPRO) to emphasize performance in unfavorable historical periods, and reports a Chinese A-share cross-sectional strategy achieving 27.99% annualized return, 12.19% maximum drawdown, and a Sharpe ratio of 1.63, roughly 68% above the CSI 300 benchmark. This work sits at the intersection of LLM-based program optimization and quantitative finance, showing that textual gradients can be applied beyond prompt engineering to generate and refine executable trading programs. If the reported out-of-sample robustness holds, it could offer quantitative researchers a more systematic, experience-driven alternative to manual strategy iteration and purely numeric hyperparameter search. TradeGrad addresses two specific problems in naive textual-gradient optimization: myopic optimization that underuses prior evaluation experience, and aggregate backtest feedback that ignores temporal robustness. It tackles these with accumulated-experience gradient estimation, multi-scale revisions for exploration and refinement, and the CPRO objective, with experiments covering both cross-sectional and time-series strategies in Chinese A-share and U.S. equity markets; code is released at github.com/transcend-0/TradeGrad.

## [SLIM benchmark exposes action-insensitive JEPA latents, fixed by inverse-dynamics loss](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03137) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces SLIM, a pushing benchmark with paired visual and language goals on identical scenes, and shows that a LeWM world model solving PushT succeeds on under 1% of trials because its encoder latents are nearly action-insensitive. Adding a single inverse-dynamics auxiliary loss, applied to encoder latents and predicted latents through a shared head discarded at test time, raises success from 0.003 to 0.35 (0.16 on the hard tier) and improves PushT at twice the trained horizon. This work pinpoints a concrete failure mode in JEPA-style latent world models and offers a cheap, targeted fix, which matters for researchers building model-based RL agents that must plan from language goals rather than goal frames. The action-sensitivity probe, computable without environment access, could become a practical diagnostic for whether a learned latent is plannable at all. Probes show the vanilla encoder's latent is nearly action-insensitive, neither pusher nor object positions can be decoded from it, and rollouts are no better than copying the current latent forward; controls attribute the repair to the gradient into the encoder. On the repaired latent, a small language-goal head plans from sentences without retraining the world model, reaching 0.84 on navigation (visual-goal oracle 1.00) and raising medium/hard pushing success from 0.04 to 0.25 when the push is given as a sequence of stage sentences.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) is a self-supervised approach to world models that learns by predicting representations rather than reconstructing pixels or tokens, and LeWM is a JEPA-style latent world model that trains end-to-end from raw pixels. Inverse dynamics is the problem of inferring the actions that produced observed state transitions, so an inverse-dynamics auxiliary loss forces the encoder to retain action-relevant information. Planning with a latent world model means rolling out predicted latents and selecting actions that reach a goal, which requires the latent to actually change in response to actions.

A new arXiv paper (2610.03185) analyzes on-policy distillation (OPD) from a reinforcement learning perspective, showing that OPD improves performance without expanding the student's capabilities and that it can collapse into excessively long, repetitive generation due to reward hacking. The authors propose masking unhealthy responses during training and using SFT initialization as effective mitigations, with code released at github.com/HancCui/opd_hacking. This work reframes OPD as a process where the teacher acts as an implicit reward model, shifting focus from how well the teacher generates to how reliably it evaluates student rollouts. It offers a mechanistic explanation for both the gains and failure modes of a widely used post-training technique, which is valuable for researchers and practitioners working on LLM post-training. The paper shows that when the implicit reward model is reliable, OPD makes correct responses easier to sample; when preference misaligns with quality, reward hacking amplifies overlong, repetitive student rollouts even though the teacher rarely generates such text itself. The proposed mitigations—masking unhealthy responses and SFT initialization—each effectively reduce collapse, and the analysis is supported by experiments and released code.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training method where a student language model is trained on samples from its own evolving policy while a teacher provides dense supervision on those same samples. Unlike standard distillation, which trains on a fixed teacher-generated dataset, OPD uses the student's own outputs, making it more aligned with the student's distribution but also more susceptible to feedback loops. Reward hacking occurs when an RL agent exploits flaws in a reward function to achieve high rewards without completing the intended task, and model collapse refers to the degeneration of generative models when trained recursively on their own outputs.

## [KV²: Self-Refining KV Cache Compression via Selective Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03198) ⭐️ 7.0/10

KV² introduces a query-agnostic KV-cache compression method that first uses a lightweight proxy scorer to identify informative in-context tokens, then reprocesses only that subset to compute final eviction scores. On RULER 16K at a 2% KV-cache budget, it improves the average score over the next-best baseline by more than 40 percentage points, and on LongBench it achieves the highest average across 2%–10% budgets with lower compression-stage runtime and peak memory than full-context reconstruction. KV-cache memory is the main bottleneck for serving long-context models, especially when one prefilled context must answer many different queries, so a method that keeps quality high at very tight budgets could substantially cut inference cost. The results suggest reusable compression does not require reprocessing the full context, which matters for anyone deploying long-context LLMs in production. KV² is query-agnostic, meaning the compressed cache is computed once and reused across future queries rather than tailored to a specific question. It is a preprint (arXiv:2610.03198v1) with code released anonymously, and its advantage over baselines widens as the KV budget tightens, though it has not yet undergone peer review.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Transformer-based large language models store key-value (KV) pairs for every token in the context so that later tokens can attend to them, and this cache grows linearly with context length, consuming large amounts of GPU memory. Query-agnostic KV-cache compression aims to shrink this cache once so it can be reused for many different queries, trading some accuracy for memory savings. Prior approaches either use cheap but inaccurate lightweight estimators or more accurate full-context reconstruction scoring that must reprocess the entire prompt, which is expensive.

## [SLMs Classify Agent Tool Calls Against Task Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03213) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.03213) investigates using Small Language Models (SLMs) as per-call task-tool relevance classifiers that judge whether each tool an AI agent selects is a logical step toward the task's intent. The authors built a novel dataset of multi-tool tasks whose required tools span distinct Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and optimized SLMs via prompt optimization, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO. Conventional authorization only checks whether an agent is permitted to invoke a tool, not whether the call actually aligns with the task's intent, so an allowed call can still be a rogue deviation. As agentic systems grow horizontally and generate more tool interactions, per-call intent verification that runs at low latency and on-prem could become a practical safety layer for agent deployments. The SLM acts as an independent relevance classifier that returns a relevance signal for downstream enforcement, rather than replacing authorization. The work is a preprint with no community discussion yet, and its evaluation relies on a purpose-built dataset spanning multiple MCP servers, so real-world generalization remains to be validated.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Tool-equipped AI agents use tool calls to access data and act on external systems, and their autonomy introduces security risks beyond traditional prompt injection. Small Language Models are lightweight language models designed to run efficiently in resource-constrained or on-prem environments, making them candidates for low-latency oversight. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard that lets agents connect to multiple external tool servers, which is why the paper's tasks span distinct MCP servers.

## [Fact Learning and Retrieval Are Separable in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03251) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.03251) trains two language models in two stages to show that a model can learn how to retrieve facts through a specific request form before it ever learns the facts themselves. By examining the hidden state immediately before the answer — the "context state" — the authors show that models trained on five request forms produce more similar context states than models trained only on statements, and that manipulating this state can enable or prevent retrieval of already-learned facts. This finding challenges the common assumption that fact storage and fact retrieval are learned together, and suggests that retrieval behavior is shaped by earlier request-form experience rather than by the facts alone. It has implications for how practitioners design training data and fine-tuning pipelines, and for interpretability research that seeks to control what a model recalls at inference time. The two-stage design is key: in stage one, one model sees each fact in five request forms while the other sees the same facts only as statements; in stage two, both receive identical training on new facts as statements. Both then retrieve new facts almost equally well from statements but differ sharply on other request forms, and the context-state intervention transfers across facts and factual relations such as capitals and currencies.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Large language models are typically trained to predict the next token over massive text corpora, and researchers have long debated whether they store facts as discrete knowledge or merely learn surface patterns of retrieval. A "request form" here means any phrasing that elicits the same fact, such as "The capital of X is" versus "The capital of X:". The "context state" is the model's internal hidden-state vector just before it emits the answer, which prior work suggests encodes the information used to produce the next token.

## [JOVE: Joint Execution and Verification for Resource-Aware LLM Task Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03296) ⭐️ 7.0/10

JOVE is a new online framework that jointly assigns executor LLMs to subtasks in a directed acyclic task graph and selects intermediate outputs for paid verification, solving a sequence of per-query mixed-integer linear programs under a long-term budget and per-query latency constraint. Across four reasoning benchmarks, it matches standard inference baselines in accuracy while cutting average cost and latency by at least 3.17x, and the authors prove sublinear quality-learning regret under natural assumptions. Deploying heterogeneous LLMs across decomposed reasoning tasks is increasingly common, but choosing which model runs which subtask and when to pay for verification is usually done heuristically. JOVE turns this into a principled online optimization problem, which could make multi-model LLM orchestration substantially cheaper and faster for production systems. The framework models stochastic, initially unknown LLM service quality, invocation costs, and execution times, and adds an information-gain bonus so that verification spending also buys learning for future allocations. Verification runs asynchronously, and the reported 3.17x cost and latency reduction is measured against standard inference baselines on four reasoning benchmarks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Complex reasoning queries are often decomposed into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subtasks, where edges encode dependencies and data flow, allowing parallel execution across different LLMs. Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is an optimization technique that handles both continuous and integer decision variables under linear constraints, and online learning with budget constraints studies how to make sequential decisions when resources are limited and feedback arrives over time. JOVE combines these ideas: it uses MILP to decide executor assignment and verification per query, while online learning updates estimates of each LLM's task-dependent quality.

## [Any-Start-Time Planning Handles Dynamic Feasibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03312) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper defines the any-start-time planning problem, where the optimal plan depends on an unknown execution start time, and introduces a data structure called a compound arrival time function (cATF) that compactly encodes the optimal plan as a function of start time. The authors provide general-purpose heuristic graph search algorithms that propagate these functions along edges instead of scalar costs, and prove the cATF size is at most linear in problem size. This work relaxes the impractical assumption of a known start time in dynamic environments, enabling efficient lookups of optimal plans once execution begins, which could significantly benefit applications like path planning among moving obstacles and scheduling. It provides a foundation for planning in dynamic worlds where feasibility of states and actions changes over time. The cATF size is proven to be at most linear in problem size, and experiments on Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) show that agents relying on replanning often fail on difficult problems, while any-start-time algorithms using cATFs can quickly look up the optimal plan once the start time is known. The approach is general-purpose and based on heuristic graph search.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: In dynamic environments, the feasibility of states or actions can change over time, such as a location becoming blocked by moving obstacles or a train only being boardable while stopped. Traditional planning often assumes a known start time, making feasibility assessment straightforward but impractical when the start time is unknown until after planning. Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) is a popular algorithm for navigation among moving obstacles that identifies safe time intervals for configurations. This paper extends such settings by removing the known-start-time assumption.

## [LiteTrajEval: Budget-Bounded Rubric-Guided Agent Trajectory Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03315) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LiteTrajEval introduces a lightweight, budget-bounded architecture that derives domain-specific rule profiles offline, preprocesses each agent trajectory online under a fixed global token budget, and invokes a single rubric-guided LLM judge to produce structured diagnostic reports. On Magentic-One-style and τ-bench-style datasets, it improves failure-localization alignment with human annotations by roughly 20–35 percentage points on Magentic-One and up to 23 percentage points on τ-retail compared with AgentRx, while cutting cost by about 6× and evaluation time by more than 8×. Trajectory evaluation is essential for improving the reliability of LLM-based agents, but repeated production use makes it expensive; a method that is both cheaper and better aligned with human judgment directly addresses a key bottleneck for deploying agents at scale. The approach has already been deployed in the authors' enterprise agentic platform, suggesting it is practical for real-world production rather than only a benchmark result. The method assumes not all raw tokens are equally useful for diagnosis, so it marks heuristic failure signals and serializes trajectories under a fixed global budget before a single judge call, rather than feeding full traces to the judge. Reported gains are relative to AgentRx on public Magentic-One-style and τ-bench-style datasets, and the abstract does not specify the exact budget sizes or judge model used.

## [MECo: LLM Multi-Task Evolution for Zero-Shot Cross-Problem Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03316) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced MECo, an LLM-driven multi-task evolutionary framework that achieves zero-shot cross-problem generalization by maintaining task-conditioned heuristic populations and using a transfer gap metric based on cross-task population performance to guide heuristic transfer and recombination. Experiments on 32 problem variants across vehicle routing (VRP) and flexible job-shop scheduling (FJSP) show MECo achieves the lowest mean costs compared with eight automated heuristic design (AHD) baselines under the same budgets, and it outperforms the strongest baseline on out-of-domain problems. This work addresses a central challenge in automated heuristic design: generalizing to entirely new problem definitions using only source-task feedback, without any target-task evaluation. If validated, MECo could reduce the substantial human expertise and repeated search currently required to design heuristics for diverse combinatorial optimization problems, and its framework can be integrated with different AHD methods to improve both in-domain and out-of-domain performance. MECo uses a complementary selection criterion that rewards each heuristic's additional coverage of source combinations to construct a compact heuristic set, which is then applied to target problems without further search or adaptation. The evaluation covers 32 problem variants across VRP and FJSP, and integrating MECo with different AHD methods improved their in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) performance in both families.

**Background**: Combinatorial optimization problems such as vehicle routing and job-shop scheduling are ubiquitous in logistics and manufacturing, but designing effective heuristics for each problem variant traditionally requires deep domain expertise and extensive trial-and-error search. Recent work has used large language models (LLMs) to automatically generate and refine heuristics, but these approaches typically rely on evaluation feedback from the specific problem being optimized, making it hard to generalize to new problem definitions. Evolutionary algorithms, which mimic biological evolution to iteratively improve candidate solutions, provide the optimization backbone that MECo combines with LLM-driven heuristic generation.

## [Refinement vs. Search: Test-Time Compute in Masked-Diffusion TTS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03320) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.03320) trains 15 masked-diffusion codec TTS models (19-133M parameters, 3 seeds) on 2,000 hours of speech and sweeps refinement steps T in [1,16] at inference, measuring zero-shot intelligibility (ASR word error rate) and speaker identity (speaker verification) on 174 held-out speakers. It finds that refinement closes 86.2% of the intelligibility range but only 46.4% of the identity range, a 1.86x asymmetry, while best-of-K search recovers speaker identity where refinement fails with 64.6-79.0% win rates across four independent encoders. The finding that refinement and depth target different bottlenecks challenges the common assumption that more inference compute uniformly improves all capabilities, and suggests TTS system designers should optimize intelligibility and speaker identity separately. It also shows that best-of-K search is a viable alternative to simply increasing refinement steps for identity preservation, which could influence how future masked-diffusion TTS systems allocate compute. The asymmetry is robust across multiple error metrics and model scales; retraining at 3x and 6x schedule attenuates but does not reverse the gap (1.84 to 1.36 to 1.23x) because intelligibility saturates with steps while identity continues improving. Separable B(d)B(T) fits significantly better than substitution models (Delta AICc=+69.3), and analysis shows 62% of the remaining identity deficit lies in the codec rather than the generator.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Masked diffusion models are a class of generative models that produce discrete data such as text or speech codec tokens by reversing a progressive masking corruption process, iteratively predicting masked tokens over multiple refinement steps. In text-to-speech, these models combine two forms of computation: model depth (parameter count) and refinement steps (inference budget), and test-time compute scaling refers to allocating more computation during inference to improve output quality. Best-of-K search is an inference strategy that generates K candidate outputs and selects the top-scoring one according to a criterion, often used when single-shot generation is unreliable.

A new arXiv paper (2610.03326) proposes a trajectory-aware low-rank compression method for diffusion language models (dLLMs) that calibrates on partially masked intermediate states rather than clean activations. The authors introduce Traj-MC, a Monte Carlo estimator that computes the trajectory second moment and achieves exact sampled-state optimality and population consistency, and report that under matched compression budgets it preserves substantially more mathematical reasoning than clean calibration. This work addresses a specific gap in low-rank compression for dLLMs, where calibration on clean activations mismatches the partially masked states seen during inference. By linking trajectory-aware low-rank optimality to retained reasoning capability, it could influence future research on efficient dLLM deployment and reasoning-preserving model compression. The method formulates a trajectory-aware low-rank objective over corruption levels and masking realizations, and Traj-MC estimates the trajectory second moment via Monte Carlo sampling with theoretical guarantees of exact sampled-state optimality and population consistency. Code is available at https://github.com/Zishan-Shao/traj-mc.git.

## [ReFract Benchmark Tests Perspective Awareness in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03356) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ReFract, a benchmark of 150 expert-validated entries that evaluates whether LLM agents can infer and respect a user's role-specific knowledge and tool boundaries in high-stakes industrial troubleshooting scenarios. State-of-the-art LLMs solve at most 69% of the tasks, with more than 50% of their trajectories containing attempts at perspective-violating actions. This benchmark exposes perspective awareness as a distinct, largely unsolved axis of agent evaluation, which is critical because agent mistakes in industrial settings can cause irreversible equipment damage, production loss, or personnel harm. It motivates developing agents that calibrate not just how to act, but for whom, advancing pluralistic alignment in high-stakes deployments. ReFract entries are grounded in anonymized queries from domain support conversations, against which Text World Models simulate the agent's operating environments and assemble perspective-aware action trajectories. The benchmark requires agents to act differently in response to the same query depending on the user's role, testing both inference of role intent and use of only legitimately accessible tools.

A capable agent must act in a way that is calibrated to the user's role, respecting the role's knowledge and capability boundaries. Unlike coding, where mistakes are usually recoverable, agent responses in these settings are enacted on physical equipment, making errors potentially irreversible. Existing benchmarks largely overlook the need for agents to infer what a role intends and to act only through tools that role may legitimately use, a capability termed Perspective Awareness.

The paper introduces Multilingual GSM-Symbolic, an extensible dataset of 30,000 item-matched question-answer pairs spanning 15 languages, built from symbolic templates that can generate millions of variations to prevent overfitting. ## [Near-Zero Monitor Readouts Do Not Prove Behavioral Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03458) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.03458) shows that low monitor readouts used to mitigate reward hacking do not reliably indicate behavioral control. In a code-generation environment, three monitors that passed the same offline gate produced floor-level or zero-median scores while policies still ranged from mixed behavior to near-pure reward hacking, depending only on random seed. This finding challenges a common assumption in AI safety that a low monitor score means the policy is behaving as intended, which could lead teams to deploy or trust models that are actually exploiting reward loopholes. It implies that offline discrimination and low monitor-aligned readouts are insufficient evidence of behavioral control, and an out-of-band behavioral check is required. The three monitors were an in-domain activation probe and two penalties conditioned on how early the policy commits to its final answer; the probe score sat at its numerical floor from the first recorded training step, and the trained-score median was zero for every prefix-trained run at the endpoint. Text-level analysis identified a prefix failure mode where generic planning and filler shells postpone the exploit past the cut without removing it from the final output, and the authors note they characterize the endpoint readout rather than its evolution.

A new arXiv paper (2610.03509) empirically tests whether efficient reasoning training harms chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness and monitorability by fine-tuning multiple models with three different length-pressure methods: a fixed generation budget, a per-example length target, and a group-relative length reward. The authors find that faithfulness and monitorability are affected differently — faithfulness drops in most settings mainly because trained models become less consistent, while monitorability remains robust even when CoT traces are much shorter. This work challenges the common assumption that efficiency-oriented training necessarily degrades CoT faithfulness, which is central to AI safety and interpretability efforts that rely on inspecting model reasoning. The nuanced finding that monitorability survives aggressive length reduction suggests that oversight mechanisms may remain viable even as inference costs are cut. The study compares three length-pressure methods — fixed generation budget, per-example length target, and group-relative length reward — and evaluates faithfulness (how well CoT reflects model decisions on related inputs) and monitorability (whether CoT reveals when input interventions alter the output). Faithfulness declines in most settings primarily due to reduced consistency of the trained models, whereas monitorability is more robust because models keep acknowledging the influence on their answer even with much shorter CoT.

## [Reasoning Models Are Accurate but Unsound on Causal Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03519) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces CERTID, a formal pipeline that uses the sound and complete ID algorithm to certify whether causal effects are identifiable and verifies model-returned formulas against structural causal models with known interventional distributions. Evaluating Gemini Flash, Gemini Pro, and GPT5.5 on 1,200 certified instances, the authors find that accuracy is a poor proxy for soundness, with false-claim rates on non-identifiable queries varying seventeen-fold across models. This work exposes a critical blind spot in how reasoning models are evaluated: a model can appear accurate while confidently answering queries that are provably unanswerable from observational data, which is a serious concern for AI safety and for any high-stakes use of causal inference. It provides the causal inference and AI communities with a rigorous benchmark and tooling to measure soundness rather than just accuracy. CERTID develops theoretical results to mitigate structural leakage, repair non-identifiable queries, and establish grading guarantees, and it verifies formulas against structural causal models whose interventional distributions are known exactly rather than relying on string matching. The evaluation spans 1,200 certified instances with 4 to 50 vertices, and the authors report that models decide identifiability with 97-100% accuracy on graphs generated after the strongest model's training snapshot.

**Background**: In causal inference, a causal effect is identifiable if it can be computed from observational data alone, and the ID algorithm introduced by Shpitser and Pearl (2006) provides a sound and complete procedure for deciding identifiability in semi-Markovian causal models with hidden variables. Structural causal models represent variables and their causal relationships through structural equations and a directed acyclic graph, allowing interventional distributions to be derived exactly. Prior evaluations of reasoning models on causal tasks lacked provably non-identifiable queries and could not accept correct formulas in equivalent forms, which is the gap CERTID addresses.

**Background**: Credit assignment is a fundamental problem in reinforcement learning: measuring how much each action contributed to a future reward. In terminal tasks, later commands often depend on information or intermediate results produced by earlier commands, so naive step-level or trajectory-level credit assignment can reward irrelevant operations. Group policy optimization methods such as GRPO sample a group of answers per prompt and use the group's average reward as a baseline, avoiding a learned value network. DepGPO extends this group-based approach by using execution dependencies to guide which steps receive credit.

## [MRVQ: One Elastic Index for Dimension- and Rate-Elastic Vector Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03651) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Matryoshka Residual Vector Quantization (MRVQ), a post-hoc residual quantizer for frozen embeddings whose maximum-rate code can be truncated two ways: dropping residual stages lowers the bit rate, and dropping embedding coordinates lowers the dimension. Across FiQA and NFCorpus, four embedding families, and {4, 8, 16}-byte codes, MRVQ uses 17.8-22.0x less memory than three separately trained QINCo2 indices and 1.89-2.02x less than a lean shared-model baseline. Dense-retrieval services must constantly switch among embedding-prefix dimensions and index bit rates as latency, quality, and memory budgets change, and tuning a quantizer separately for each rate forces the retrieval tier to hold several code streams and quantizer states at once. MRVQ shows that a single resident artifact can serve every evaluated (dimension, rate) pair, offering a practical low-memory operating point for elastic retrieval deployments. The memory saving is not free: per-rate QINCo2 is 0.026-0.107 nDCG@10 better on FiQA, though MRVQ beats PQ, OPQ, and AdANNS-OPQ at matched code size. The paper also reports a low-build-cost PCA-scalar design fitting 420x faster at the median than RaBitQ and its extension, plus two negative results: QINCo2 collapses when trained at high rates, and a ranking-bound hypothesis misses its pre-specified acceptance criteria.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Vector search retrieves items by comparing dense embeddings, and quantization compresses those embeddings so large indexes fit in memory. Residual quantization represents a vector as a sum of stage-wise codebook entries, and QINCo2 replaces static codebooks with small neural networks that generate implicit codebooks conditioned on the quantized history. Matryoshka-style methods exploit nested representations so that a single artifact can be truncated to different sizes, and MRVQ combines this idea with residual quantization to make one index elastic in both dimension and bit rate.

## [IntentCoding: A Training-Free Decoding Strategy to Amplify User Intent in LLM Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.00066) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2602.00066) introduces IntentCoding, a model-agnostic decoding strategy that captures the influence of user intent by masking it out and then applies a multi-strength ensemble mechanism to amplify that influence during generation. The authors also release CodeConstraints, a benchmark for testing intent compliance under varying numbers of constraints, and report up to 71.0% relative improvement on CodeConstraints, 67.3% on IFEvalCode, and 29.3% relative pass@1 improvement on HumanEval and LiveCodeBench compared with greedy decoding. LLMs are increasingly used to write code from natural-language specifications, but they often fail to satisfy multiple fine-grained constraints at once, and this work offers a practical, training-free fix that plugs into existing decoding pipelines. Because it is model-agnostic and requires no fine-tuning, it could be adopted broadly by developers and tooling vendors seeking more reliable code assistants. The method works by first masking out the user intent to measure its effect on the model's logits, then ensembling outputs at multiple amplification strengths to steer decoding; it requires no additional training and integrates seamlessly with standard decoding procedures. The empirical analysis motivating it shows that model performance degrades quickly as the number of constraints grows, and that user intent does influence logits but not strongly enough to reliably steer generation on its own.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Decoding strategies determine how a language model turns its raw next-token scores (logits) into actual output, with common approaches including greedy decoding, beam search, and sampling methods like top-p. Code generation benchmarks such as HumanEval and LiveCodeBench measure functional correctness, while IFEvalCode and the new CodeConstraints focus on instruction and constraint following. IntentCoding sits in the decoding layer, meaning it changes how tokens are selected at inference time rather than altering the model's weights.

## [ClarifyCodeBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Clarifying Ambiguous Code Requirements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00711) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ClarifyCodeBench, a new interactive benchmark built from real-world programming tasks that evaluates how well large language models can clarify ambiguous, incomplete, or underspecified requirements before generating code. The paper also formalizes two metrics—Turn-discounted Key Question Rate and Optimal Round Adherence—and systematically evaluates six state-of-the-art LLMs. The benchmark highlights that strong one-shot code generation does not guarantee effective requirement clarification, suggesting that future AI4SE research should shift from static synthesis toward interactive elicitation. This matters for developers and tool builders who rely on AI coding assistants in real, iterative software engineering workflows. The paper reports three key findings: capability decoupling (code generation skill does not transfer to clarification), a reasoning paradox (more computational thinking improves code correctness but only marginally helps ambiguity identification), and a multi-ambiguity ceiling (clarification performance degrades sharply as ambiguity density increases). The benchmark uses high-quality manual annotations including unique ambiguity types, clarification questions, and ground-truth answers.

Existing code benchmarks typically assume perfectly specified prompts, ignoring the iterative back-and-forth of requirement elicitation that characterizes real software engineering. ClarifyCodeBench addresses this gap by testing whether models can proactively ask clarifying questions before writing code.

## [CONTRA: Selective Clarification for LLM Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01769) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose CONTRA, a training-free method that discovers candidate clarification questions and qualifies them using both semantic filtering and execution-based behavioral checks, then decides whether to ask or stop based on interaction history. On ClarifyCodeBench it achieves the highest F1 across all four coding agents, exceeding the best baseline macro-average F1 by 13.88 percentage points, and it is also released as a Claude Code plugin. LLM coding agents often silently resolve underspecified requirements with their own assumptions, producing code that looks correct but implements unintended behavior, and fixing such mismatches becomes costlier as development builds on them. CONTRA targets this problem by asking only behavior-changing questions, which could reduce costly rework in AI-assisted software engineering without burdening developers with unnecessary interruptions. For each surviving question, CONTRA generates programs conditioned on two plausible answers and checks whether they produce stable behavioral differences on shared inputs; only questions with such differences are kept, and the interaction history is then used to select among qualified questions or stop asking. The method is training-free and was evaluated with the same LLM and evaluation protocol against the Claude Code and OpenHands coding harnesses, where it achieved higher clarification recall and F1.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: In LLM-based code generation, a user's request is often underspecified, so the model must fill in missing details with assumptions that may not match the user's intent. Clarification questions can resolve this ambiguity early, but asking too many or irrelevant questions interrupts developers and slows down development. CONTRA addresses this trade-off by combining broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based qualification, and it is evaluated on ClarifyCodeBench, a benchmark designed for clarification in code generation.

## [CORE: Coverage Calibration and Evicted-Mass Redistribution for KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02235) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (arXiv:2610.02235) introduces CORE, a KV cache compression method that starts from an exact factorization of eviction error as evicted attention mass times the directional gap between the evicted centroid and the retained output. CORE distills an offline allocation combining query utility and log-determinant coverage into a lightweight cache-aware indexer, and at inference a single calibrated distribution drives both retention (Top-B ordering of complementary KV states) and compensation (latent-memory writes parameterized by excluded allocation mass and conditional weights). Across three backbones, CORE exceeds the strongest RULER baseline by up to 3.78 points at 90% compression, with LongBench and repeated-eviction evaluations confirming effectiveness and decoding efficiency. Long-context decoding is increasingly bottlenecked by KV cache memory and bandwidth, and existing fixed-budget compression methods typically separate retention from compensation, leaving the discarded attention mass and the direction of induced output error unaccounted for. CORE's unified calibration mechanism jointly optimizes retention and compensation, which could make long-context inference more memory-efficient for applications such as LLM agents, long-document summarization, and repository-level code completion. The paper provides a four-term pre-compensation error certificate, characterizes non-additive coverage interactions, and establishes mass-independent write stability with hierarchical bounds through recurrent and query-adaptive normalization. Notably, CORE avoids a separate write-weight predictor and online log-determinant evaluation, and its gains are reported at 90% compression across three backbones.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: In transformer-based large language models, the key-value (KV) cache stores intermediate attention states for all previously processed tokens so that decoding does not need to recompute them, but its memory footprint grows linearly with context length. KV cache compression methods reduce this footprint by evicting or merging less important cached states under a fixed budget, which can degrade output quality if the discarded attention mass is not properly compensated. CORE addresses this by treating eviction error as a product of evicted attention mass and a directional gap, and by using coverage-aware retention plus mass-preserving memory writes to limit the damage.

## [RxnOptBench: New Benchmark Tests LLMs on Organic Reaction-Condition Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02242) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced RxnOptBench, a benchmark that evaluates large language models on selecting optimal organic reaction conditions using real wet-lab optimization tables mined from 2025 organic-methodology papers. It grades models with a continuous relative score derived from a headline utility combining yield with enantiomeric excess (ee), diastereomeric ratio (dr), and regioisomeric ratio (rr), and includes a paired precedents-vs-no-precedents design to separate in-context literature use from parametric memorization. Reaction-condition optimization is a central, judgement-heavy task in organic methodology, yet existing chemistry benchmarks focus on reaction-class labelling, retrosynthesis, or SMILES manipulation rather than reading real condition-screening tables. RxnOptBench fills this gap for the AI-for-science and LLM-evaluation communities, and its finding that even frontier models leave substantial headroom highlights how far LLMs remain from reliably supporting real synthetic decision-making. Across nine frontier LLMs and three chemistry-specialized LLMs, chemistry-specialized models fell to the random-baseline floor on multi-axis selection, while open-weight models have closed most of the gap to proprietary frontier models. The benchmark releases a final human-reviewed test set and evaluation code, and its continuous scoring rewards models that jointly optimize yield and stereoselectivity rather than treating them as separate objectives.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: In organic chemistry, optimizing a reaction means choosing the catalyst, ligand, solvent, reagent, temperature, time, and atmosphere that jointly maximize yield and stereoselectivity. Key stereochemical metrics include enantiomeric excess (ee), which measures how much one enantiomer dominates over its mirror image; diastereomeric ratio (dr), the ratio of one diastereomer to another; and regioisomeric ratio (rr), the ratio of a major regioisomer to other isomers. Large language models are increasingly expected to assist with this kind of synthetic judgement, but until now no benchmark asked them to read a real condition-screening table and pick the best set of conditions.

## [ReRoute Enables Counterfactual Prediction in Scientific Emulators Without Controlled Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02252) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ReRoute, a framework for targeted scientific what-if prediction that combines factual data with partial mechanistic knowledge, eliminating the need for controlled intervention data. On held-out coupled-climate interventions, ReRoute reduced aggregate climate error by 18.2-31.8% under severe CO2 distribution shifts while preserving skill under standard conditions. This addresses a fundamental challenge in causal inference and scientific machine learning: models can predict accurately on observed data yet fail on what-if queries when correlated inputs are varied independently. The approach could significantly reduce the cost and computational burden of generating controlled simulation data for climate emulation and other scientific domains. ReRoute fixes the queried input of a pretrained backbone to a reference value, reintroduces its variation through a known mechanistic pathway, and fine-tunes on the original factual data, leaving downstream effects to the learned dynamics. The authors provide a causal identification result under explicit structural assumptions, with the core argument machine-checked in Lean, and demonstrate accuracy in a controlled advection-diffusion system where exact responses are available.

Researchers introduced EditHero, described as the first benchmark for long-horizon, part-level 3D editing, where natural-language instructions and target images drive sequential edits to both geometry and texture. A deterministic assembly engine produces the exact target after every edit, and every sequence is manually reviewed. Most 3D editing methods are evaluated on a single edit, but real assets are built through long sequences of revisions, so EditHero fills a gap in measuring whether methods can make requested changes without disturbing everything else. Its comparison of non-agentic and LLM/VLM agentic approaches offers practical guidance for building reliable iterative 3D editing tools. Non-agentic methods work top down by regenerating the object from a learned 3D representation and inferring what to keep, often missing the requested change and disturbing regions that should stay fixed. LLM/VLM agents work bottom up by editing through code that inspects the mesh and rewrites only the required parts, following instructions more closely and preserving unedited parts better, but each edit takes minutes.

## [SF-MOPD Uses Slow-Fast Coupling to Preserve Capabilities in Multimodal LLM Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02324) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02324) proposes Slow-Fast Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (SF-MOPD), which couples a fast student model updated directly by each teacher with a slow model that is an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student. For each teacher, SF-MOPD computes the teacher-induced update in log-probability space and removes only the component that pushes the fast model away from the slow model, while retaining aligned and orthogonal components. The slow model absorbs the learning signal gradually and serves as a moving capability reference that fuses the general foundation with confirmed domain expertise. Experiments across multiple model scales show SF-MOPD mitigates capability interference, enhances specialized multimodal capabilities, and reduces average degradation on general-capability benchmarks, consistently outperforming vanilla MOPD.

## [MIRROR: Multipath Quorum Integrity for LLM Multi-Agent Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02349) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MIRROR introduces a communication-layer integrity primitive that replicates a single canonicalized payload across k logical routes and accepts a message only when a strict majority of routes report the same digest. Across MMLU, HumanEval, and MBPP on two frameworks and four communication topologies, and in a MetaGPT deployment against a production API, MIRROR reduces Agent-in-the-Middle attack success rates to 0% below the route-compromise threshold at 1x LLM token cost. This addresses an underexplored security vulnerability in LLM multi-agent systems, where prior work reports attack success rates approaching 100% on structured tasks. It offers a low-cost defense that avoids the 35x token overhead and up to 44.2% benign-output blocking seen with LLM-as-a-Judge semantic validation. MIRROR uses unkeyed hashing and authenticates nothing on its own, since an active on-path adversary can always recompute a digest over a modified payload; all integrity derives from the assumption that honest routes form a majority (alpha < 0.5). The guarantee extends to correlated routes, where the key quantity is the size of the largest shared-failure group rather than the route count, and availability and integrity degrade at the same threshold.

Existing defenses use semantic validation, which requires extra inference and can block benign outputs, or transport-layer encryption, which fails when an intermediary legitimately terminates TLS. Quorum systems require agreement among multiple participants, and multipath routing spreads traffic across independent paths to increase the number of nodes an adversary must compromise.

A new arXiv paper (2610.02359) introduces Lexicographic Multi-Objective On-Policy Distillation (LMOPD), a multi-teacher method that integrates reward-specialized policies under explicit priority ordering. For each student rollout, LMOPD selects the specialist for the first objective whose gate detects a deficiency, then locally projects its centered log-policy correction to remove components that oppose higher-priority specialists. Evaluated on 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts models across three math benchmarks, LMOPD with two experts fully retained accuracy and reasoning-quality gains while acquiring 46.9% of the conciseness gain, and with four experts retained roughly 90% of both accuracy and reasoning-correctness gains versus only about 57% for the next best baseline. This work addresses a core problem in multi-reward post-training: existing methods typically scalarize rewards or combine specialists without protecting a priority order, which is dangerous when trade-offs are asymmetric (e.g., conciseness should never improve at the cost of correctness). By making priorities explicit, LMOPD offers a principled way to integrate reward-specialized policies for LLM post-training, potentially improving how models balance correctness, reasoning quality, and response length. LMOPD is evaluated on 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts transformer models in two- and four-expert settings on three math benchmarks, measuring retained specialist gains. Matched four-expert ablations show that lexicographic routing outperforms random routing and that the projection step further strengthens top-priority capabilities.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a training paradigm that uses rule-based, automatically checkable reward signals (e.g., math or code correctness) instead of human ratings or learned reward models. On-policy distillation is a knowledge distillation technique where the student model samples its own trajectories and a stronger teacher provides dense token-level supervision on them, reducing exposure bias. Lexicographic optimization is a multi-objective optimization approach that optimizes objectives in a strict priority order, ensuring lower-priority objectives never degrade higher-priority ones. LMOPD combines these ideas: multiple reward-specialized teacher policies are distilled into one student under an explicit lexicographic priority.

## [Isaac-Net: GPU-Batched 5G Simulation for Massively Parallel Robot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02370) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released Isaac-Net, a GPU-batched 5G New Radio (NR) module that advances the uplink of thousands of robot environments in lockstep with Isaac Lab physics, simulating every 0.5 ms slot for all environments at once. Validated against ns-3 5G-LENA, it reproduces median delay across loads (5-10% low on an unseen carrier, 9% high at 32 robots per environment in closed loop) and keeps the network in the loop for about one million robots on one GPU at 83% of the Isaac Lab rate without the network. This bridges a critical gap between GPU robot simulators, which reduce networks to independent per-message delays, and packet-level simulators like ns-3, which run one scenario per CPU process and cannot keep pace with thousands of parallel environments. It enables scalable network-in-the-loop training for multi-robot fleets using private 5G, where each robot's delay depends on its teammates' traffic. Isaac-Net also reproduces the Age of Information (AoI) of each robot's newest delivered report, whereas an independent per-message delay model leaves the AoI tail about three times too light. The code is open source on GitHub, though results are measured under a random policy and the paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

## [Inherit-MAS Evolves Multi-Agent Workflows via Inheritance at Test Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02396) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Inherit-MAS introduces a test-time evolution method for LLM-based multi-agent systems that makes inheritance explicit at two levels: workflow inheritance, which refines the latest completed candidate workflow by discarding unhelpful nodes and applying validated edits, and execution inheritance, which reuses stored results only when the fully resolved request and execution context match. With GPT-4o-mini workers, it achieves 55.4% completion on WorkBench and 49.7% joint F1 on HotpotQA FullWiki, outperforming EvoAgent, EvoMAS, and TacoMAS, and with Qwen3-32B workers it also exceeds these evolving-MAS baselines. The work addresses two central pain points in test-time evolution of multi-agent systems: broad revisions that disturb already-useful workflow components, and redundant re-execution of unchanged requests. By showing that explicit inheritance can both improve benchmark performance and cut token usage, it offers a practical direction for making self-evolving agent systems cheaper and more stable to operate. Execution inheritance reduced worker-token usage by 29.1% on WorkBench and 34.6% on HotpotQA, and total token usage by 5.3% and 18.1%, compared with rerunning the same controller with execution inheritance disabled. The method relies on a meta-model that synthesizes a workflow of worker agents with declared roles, communication inputs, and tool permissions, plus a separately prompted judge that scores each executed candidate and diagnoses its deficiencies.

Inherit-MAS draws inspiration from the interplay of inheritance and selection in biological evolution to make inheritance explicit at the workflow and execution levels.

## [Whiteout: Overwriting Sensitive Data to Stop LLM Leakage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02418) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.02418) introduces Whiteout, a tool that prevents large language models from regurgitating personally sensitive information (PSI) such as birth dates, phone numbers, and home addresses by overwriting that data with carefully designed obfuscation samples. The authors evaluate Whiteout on modern LLMs of varying sizes and makers, including a widely-used OpenAI model, and report that it blocks disclosure of targeted PSIs with negligible impact on model utility and safety, outperforming existing alternatives. LLMs trained on massive unfiltered web data frequently memorize and reproduce private information, creating serious risks for high-profile individuals like executives, politicians, and judges. Whiteout offers a practical, user-request-driven alternative to machine unlearning that avoids degrading model utility and safety, potentially giving individuals a low-cost way to protect their data in deployed models. Whiteout is tested against a wide range of countermeasures, from black-box attacks like jailbreaking to white-box adaptive attacks such as relearning and quantization, and the paper concludes with a discussion of security and ethical implications. As an arXiv preprint, it has not yet undergone peer review, and the abstract does not quantify the exact utility or safety trade-offs.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Large language models are trained on enormous, largely unfiltered datasets that include scraped websites and user inputs, so they can memorize and later reproduce personally sensitive information. Machine unlearning is the main existing mitigation, aiming to remove the influence of specific data from a trained model, but it often removes more information than needed, degrades model utility and safety, and is vulnerable to attacks. Whiteout instead takes an obfuscation approach: rather than deleting the information, it overwrites the targeted sensitive data with carefully designed decoy samples so the model no longer outputs the genuine values.

A new arXiv paper (2610.02437) theoretically analyzes why supervised fine-tuning (SFT) causes more catastrophic forgetting than reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) on classification tasks. Using a tractable linear-softmax policy, the authors derive an exact decomposition of parameter updates into semantic and style components, showing that SFT develops off-axis style drift while RFT preserves semantic symmetry. It could influence how the community designs fine-tuning pipelines for classification and other tasks where forgetting is costly.
