## [LayerRoute: Action-Conditioned Mixture-of-Layers Routing for VLA Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06079) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LayerRoute introduces an action-conditioned representation routing interface for Vision-Language-Action policies, combining a Layer Mixture Router that dynamically forms mixtures of cached VLM layer representations with an Action-State Reread mechanism that explicitly reuses earlier action representations. Across simulation and real-world benchmarks it consistently improves StarVLA-π and π0.5, gaining up to 7.2 points on LIBERO Long with only 0.31% / 3.87% additional parameters. Existing VLA interfaces expose VLM information through fixed layer assignments for each action layer and propagate intermediate action states only implicitly, which limits how flexibly a policy can draw on hierarchical visual-semantic features. The method relies on cached VLM representations and a router that forms mixtures on the fly, plus an Action-State Reread path that explicitly reuses earlier action representations rather than relying solely on residual streams. Ablation studies confirm the benefit of action-conditioned layer routing, and routing analyses reveal structured allocation patterns across action layers and task settings, though the reported gains are largest on LIBERO Long and the added parameters remain small.

A new arXiv paper (arXiv:2609.15054v2) proposes BusMA, a communication framework that replaces hierarchical Manager-Worker (HMW) and Router-based Message Passing (RMP) protocols with a shared channel called the Bus, allowing any agent to directly address any peer. BusMA comprises agent registration, message routing, and shared memory management, and introduces four communication intents—discussion, challenge, guidance, and request for explanation—coordinated by a Chair agent that monitors shared memory to drive convergence. By letting workers consult specific peers directly through a shared bus, BusMA points to a more flexible, fault-tolerant design pattern that could influence how future multi-agent LLM frameworks and orchestration libraries are built. The framework is inspired by computer bus architectures, where multiple devices communicate over a shared pathway managed by arbitration protocols rather than routed packets. Each worker agent has its own local memory and tools, and can reason, act, and post shared messages with specific intents; the Chair agent only coordinates rather than dictating task decomposition. The evaluation covers 13 tasks and two frontier LLMs, but the paper is an incremental research contribution rather than a paradigm shift, and no community discussion is available to validate its real-world impact.

## [Checkpoint Handoff Protocol Separates Reaching from Solving in Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19636) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.19636v2) introduces checkpoint handoff, an evaluation protocol that decouples an agent's ability to reach useful states from its ability to complete tasks without retraining. One checkpoint acts as a reacher up to a handoff point, and another continues as the solver from the same replayed history, with Reach and Solve measured separately across two benchmarks and two independently released training pipelines. Final task success conflates two distinct capabilities, so prior comparisons of language-model agents may have misattributed RL gains to better decision-making rather than better state-reaching. This protocol lets agentic RL evaluations report arrival and completion alongside final success, giving researchers a more precise way to diagnose where reinforcement learning actually helps. Reach measures how often a reacher arrives at states that a replayable environment verifies to be a fixed number of actions from success, while Solve measures how often a solver completes the task from identical cloned copies of those states. Across three model scales on TravelPlanner and both ALFWorld splits, the solver gain from switching SFT to RL is consistently larger when RL is the reacher, and separately measured Reach and Solve gaps recover most of this difference.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning is widely used to improve language-model agents that act over many steps in interactive environments, and progress is typically judged by whether the agent eventually completes the task. However, because an agent's earlier actions determine the states its later decisions face, final success mixes together the ability to get somewhere useful with the ability to finish once there. Checkpoint handoff borrows the idea of a replayable environment — one that exposes reset and step interfaces so recorded decision points can be replayed — to isolate these two factors.

The paper proposes T^5, a twin-critic method that calibrates token-level advantages from a single generated trajectory during reinforcement mid-training. The method uses warmup and held-out qualification for the critics, and a signal-retention constraint prevents the correction from erasing the learning signal. Theoretically, the paper characterizes optimal mixing under this constraint and establishes an upper bound on residual mean-induced drift.

SafeCoEvo introduces a test-time Harness-Guard co-evolution framework that lets an LLM agent's external safety system adapt using only runtime experience accumulated from past tasks. It jointly improves two complementary capabilities: S-Harness rapidly externalizes recent experience into updatable explicit safety knowledge, while GuardVPO internalizes accumulated safety experience over a longer timescale into parametric risk-judgment abilities, reducing unsafe outcome rate by 10.05% and raising task success rate by 12.15% over the strongest baseline. The framework separates adaptation into two timescales: short-term rapid adaptation via S-Harness, which produces explicit, updatable safety knowledge that can immediately influence subsequent tasks, and long-term consolidation via GuardVPO, which turns accumulated runtime safety experience into parametric risk-judgment capability. The reported gains are measured against the strongest baseline, with a 10.05% reduction in unsafe outcomes and a 12.15% improvement in task success rate.

## [PTNO Trains Neural Operators on Noisy Monte Carlo Labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40090) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the Particle Transport Neural Operator (PTNO), a neural operator that learns particle transport surrogates directly from noisy, low-cost Monte Carlo (MC) labels rather than expensive converged solutions. It shows that because MC labels are unbiased, the squared loss on noisy labels shares its minimizer with the loss on converged solutions, and it handles high dynamic range via a softplus output layer plus a pointwise relative L2 (PRelL2) loss. On two neutronics tasks PTNO is 10^4-10^5x faster than converged MC on the same CPU and 10^3-10^5x cheaper at matched accuracy, while on two radiative-transfer tasks MC at matched accuracy costs 0.8-11x as much as PTNO. This work could substantially lower the cost of high-fidelity particle transport simulation in radiative transfer and plasma physics, where converged Monte Carlo runs are prohibitively expensive. By showing that many cheap noisy scenes can beat fewer converged ones, it offers a practical recipe for amortizing simulation cost in scientific machine learning, relevant to fusion reactor neutronics and participating-media rendering. The budget-allocation study over training scenes M, MC samples per render N, and independent renders per scene K shows that many noisy scenes beat fewer converged ones, and the authors avoid nonlinear transforms like the logarithm because they bias noisy supervision. PTNO instead keeps labels in physical space, enforces positivity with a softplus output layer, and uses PRelL2, which normalizes each residual by the stop-gradient prediction rather than the noisy label.

By exposing and mitigating a concrete reward-collapse mechanism, this work could improve the stability and token efficiency of RL training for reasoning models, affecting researchers and practitioners who rely on GRPO-style pipelines. The paper shows that under GRPO-based settings, PCP makes probability-based rewards nearly indistinguishable, destabilizing and slowing policy optimization; RLCPR counters this with two components: uncertainty-aware data sampling that reduces concentration-prone rollouts before generation, and concentration-aware regularization that penalizes unnecessarily long traces when posterior rewards collapse. The reported gains come alongside higher token efficiency, though the abstract does not detail the exact benchmarks or model scales used.

The paper introduces Causal Memory Policy (CMP), a causal framework that intervenes on retrieval itself by reserving a fixed number of context slots for memories sampled with known propensities, thereby restoring identification of memory utility in memory-augmented LLMs. It proves causal factorization, unbiasedness and exact variance of a self-normalized inverse propensity weighting estimator, and an optimal decision rule under irreversible operations, while empirically showing identification fails for 54% of required memories on LongMemEval and 67% on LoCoMo. This work addresses a fundamental identification problem in memory-augmented LLMs, where utility estimates rely solely on retrieved memories and thus become invisible when memories are never retrieved, affecting the reliability of retention decisions. CMP improves discrimination between required and non-required memories from 0.54 to 0.66 AUC, but the paper notes that identified memory utility alone is insufficient for retention decisions: per-query utility reaches 0.78 AUC on the query for which it is estimated, yet no aggregation available to a retention policy predicts a memory's value on unseen queries. Testing 11 LLMs, the authors find that RAG is not always better than non-RAG, that more retrieved documents can hurt performance, and that document order can affect results. The findings challenge the common assumption that adding retrieval always improves LLM outputs, showing that the decision to adopt RAG should be made case-by-case. This has direct implications for practitioners building RAG-based applications, who must weigh retrieval quality, document count, and ordering rather than assuming more context is better. The paper introduces three robustness metrics corresponding to its three research questions, and finds that Qwen and GPT models show notable robustness declines when reasoning is disabled, even on single-hop QA. Providing retrieved documents as tool responses improves Claude models but hurts Qwen and GPT models, despite GPT models having the best overall robustness under vanilla prompting.

## [C-EDL: Post-hoc Conflict-Aware Method Boosts Adversarial and OOD Robustness of Evidential Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05937) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Conflict-aware Evidential Deep Learning (C-EDL), a lightweight post-hoc uncertainty quantification approach that enhances adversarial and out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness of Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) without retraining. C-EDL generates diverse task-preserving transformations per input and quantifies representational disagreement to calibrate uncertainty estimates, achieving up to ~55% reduction in coverage for OOD data and up to ~90% for adversarial data across multiple datasets and attack types. EDL is an efficient uncertainty quantification paradigm but is particularly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, leading to overconfident errors that can be detrimental in high-stakes applications such as autonomous driving or medical diagnosis. C-EDL addresses this critical weakness with low computational overhead and no retraining, making it practical for deployment in safety-critical systems and potentially improving trustworthiness of deep learning models. C-EDL is a post-hoc method that operates on a single forward pass and introduces conflict-aware prediction adjustment to improve detection of OOD and adversarial inputs while maintaining high in-distribution accuracy. The approach is evaluated across a range of datasets, attack types, and uncertainty metrics, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art EDL variants and competitive baselines.

A new arXiv paper (2507.07871) proposes a randomized watermark key selection defense that provides a sample-count-independent upper bound on forgery success for blind attackers, without degrading model utility. The method randomizes key selection per query and accepts content as genuine only if exactly one key detects the watermark, reducing harmful-text forgery success from up to 87% with a single key to as low as 1% with four keys. Watermark forgery threatens the trustworthiness of AI content provenance, as adversaries can insert a provider's watermark into content they did not generate, damaging reputation and undermining verification systems. This defense is modality-agnostic and can be applied to any existing watermarking method as a black-box, making it broadly practical for GenAI providers without redesigning their schemes. The guarantee is conditional on key-symmetric, independent detector outcomes and applies to blind attackers; the method treats the underlying watermarking method as a black-box and does not rely on computational hardness assumptions like cryptographic watermarks. A preliminary image study using Tree-Ring shows forgery success dropping from 100% to 2%, with negligible computational overhead.

A new arXiv paper (2508.17497v3) proposes Relation-Conditioned Multimodal Learning (RCML), a framework that learns multimodal representations conditioned on natural-language relation descriptions instead of producing a single relation-agnostic embedding per sample. Researchers propose Cocoon, a system architecture that efficiently handles the large noise history required by correlated-noise differentially private training by distributing storage and computation across CPU, GPU, and memory extension modules, including near-memory processing (NMP) devices. On a real system with an FPGA-based NMP prototype, Cocoon achieves 1.23–10.82x performance improvements over baselines. Differentially private training is essential for protecting sensitive data in machine learning, but correlated-noise mechanisms that improve accuracy incur significant overhead when models or embedding tables are large. Cocoon addresses this bottleneck with hardware-aware optimizations, potentially making accurate and scalable DP-ML more practical for real-world deployment. Cocoon introduces optimizations for sparse embedding tables and leverages to-be-commercialized near-memory processing devices to store and process the noise history. The evaluation is based on an FPGA-based NMP prototype, and the reported speedups range from 1.23x to 10.82x depending on model size and hardware capacity.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Differential privacy (DP) provides formal guarantees that individual training examples cannot be inferred from a model, but standard DP training algorithms like DP-SGD add independent noise at each iteration, which degrades accuracy. A newer family of mechanisms adds correlated noise across iterations so that the noise cancels out, improving utility, but these methods require storing and processing a long history of noise vectors, creating a systems bottleneck. Cocoon is a hardware-software co-designed framework that tackles this bottleneck by distributing the noise history across CPU, GPU, and memory extension modules, including near-memory processing (NMP) devices that place computation closer to memory.

## [Analytically Tractable Model Explains LLM Inference-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.19905) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2512.19905v3) introduces an analytically tractable model of inference-time scaling based on Bayesian linear regression with a reward-weighted sampler, where the reward comes from a linear model that mimics the LLM-as-a-judge setting. The authors derive closed-form expressions for the posterior predictive mean and variance in the high-dimensional regime and analyze how generalization error depends on the number of inference samples k, the sampling temperature, and reward misspecification. Inference-time scaling is increasingly used to boost LLM performance by spending more compute at test time, but its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. This work provides provable conditions under which scaling inference compute beats collecting more training data, and shows when it can actually hurt, offering guidance for practitioners designing sampling and reward strategies. The analysis shows that when the reward is not too different from the teacher, generalization error decreases monotonically with more inference samples k, but the reward that optimizes selection generally differs from the teacher. Substantial reward misspecification creates a finite optimal k beyond which more sampling increases error, and for fixed k there exists an optimal sampling temperature; in the best-of-k limit with the teacher as reward, error decays as Θ(1/k^2), with the leading coefficient derived via extreme value theory.

**Background**: Inference-time scaling (also called test-time compute scaling) means allocating more computation during inference, for example by generating many candidate answers and selecting the best one, rather than only scaling model size or training data. LLM-as-a-judge is a common technique where one LLM scores or ranks the outputs of another, often used as a cheaper alternative to human evaluation. It finds that plain VGG-style stacks show early accuracy saturation as D_eff grows, while ResNet and GoogLeNet keep D_eff low relative to nominal depth and continue to benefit from added depth — a pattern the authors call the "Effective Depth Paradox." The results suggest that architectural topology, not raw layer count, governs trainability and scaling efficiency in deep CNNs, offering practitioners a cheap pre-training metric for reasoning about depth. This could inform architecture design choices and help explain why nominally deeper residual networks can be easier to train than shallower sequential ones. Pooled correlation analysis shows both nominal depth (r = 0.94) and effective depth (r = 0.93) are strongly associated with accuracy (both p < 0.01), but the small family-clustered sample cannot cleanly separate the two metrics, so gradient-norm evidence is treated as complementary rather than decisive.

## [Goldilocks RL tunes task difficulty to escape sparse rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14868) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2602.14868v3) introduces Goldilocks, an adaptive data-selection strategy that trains a Selector network to predict the standard deviation of rewards across a language model's rollouts for each candidate question, prioritizing questions with high predicted reward variability. Trained with GRPO on the OpenMathReasoning and Polaris datasets, Goldilocks consistently outperforms standard GRPO, requiring up to 78% fewer optimization steps to match its performance. Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning for language model reasoning highly sample-inefficient, and Goldilocks offers a practical way to improve sample efficiency at the large scale of modern LLM training. If it generalizes, it could reduce the compute cost of RL-based reasoning training and make such methods more accessible. The Selector is trained on the model's performance on seen samples, so it continuously adapts to the model's evolving abilities, and it targets questions that are neither too easy nor too hard (the Goldilocks principle). The approach is evaluated on the OpenMathReasoning and Polaris datasets and is a preprint without community discussion yet.

## [DLM-AN: Controllable Accent Normalization via Discrete Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14275) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose DLM-AN, a controllable accent normalization system built on masked discrete diffusion over self-supervised speech tokens, which uses a Common Token Predictor to selectively reuse source tokens and thereby tune accent strength. A flow-matching Duration Ratio Predictor automatically adjusts total duration to match native rhythm, and experiments on multi-accent English data show DLM-AN achieves the lowest word error rate among all compared systems. Most existing accent normalization methods offer no control over accent strength, yet applications like language learning and dubbing need tunable accent retention, so DLM-AN's smooth and interpretable control fills a practical gap. Its state-of-the-art word error rate on multi-accent English also suggests discrete diffusion over self-supervised speech tokens is a competitive alternative to conventional accent conversion pipelines. The accent strength control is achieved simply by reusing more or fewer source tokens to initialize the reverse diffusion process, where reusing more tokens preserves more of the original accent. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/P1ping/DLM-AN, and the approach delivers competitive accent reduction alongside the lowest WER.

## [PALM Finds Compact LLM Portfolios for Multi-Objective Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04144) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2604.04144v3) introduces PALM (Portfolio of Aligned LLMs), an algorithm that combines a structured grid of reward weight vectors, a lazy search that optimizes policies only where needed, and pruning to return a small portfolio of LLM policies. Given target approximation tolerances, PALM provably contains a near-optimal policy for every weight vector, with an explicit upper bound on portfolio size, and experiments show it generally achieves smaller approximation gaps than same-size portfolios built from uniformly spaced or randomly sampled weights. Multi-objective alignment typically forces teams to train and deploy many separate policies for different trade-offs between helpfulness, harmlessness, and conciseness, which is expensive. PALM's compact, provably near-optimal portfolio could make scalable personalization, reward-weight exploration during development, and compact decoding-time configurations far more practical for LLM deployment. PALM provides an explicit upper bound on portfolio size and scales to higher-dimensional reward spaces through efficient search and sparse preference structure, but it relies on target approximation tolerances specified by the user and assumes reward functions across the relevant dimensions are available. The paper reports that its portfolios outperform uniformly spaced or randomly sampled weight portfolios of the same size in terms of approximation gap.

A new arXiv paper (2604.10800v2) introduces a unified cross-language vulnerability lifecycle framework combining LLM-driven hybrid structural-semantic detection, execution-grounded agentic validation, and validation-aware iterative repair, governed by a strict invariant that no repair is applied without execution-based confirmation of exploitability. The strong zero-shot cross-language performance and explainability from learned gating weights also suggest practical value for multi-language software security workflows. Cross-language generalization is achieved via a Universal Abstract Syntax Tree (uAST) that normalizes Java, Python, and C++ into a shared structural schema, combined with a hybrid fusion of GraphSAGE and Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B embeddings through learned two-way gating that provides intrinsic per-sample explainability. Ablations show removing uAST degrades cross-language F1 by 23.42%, while disabling validation increases unnecessary repairs by 131.7%.

## [Dual-Certified White-Box Inference for Input Convex Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04722) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces dual-certified inference (DCI) for second-order cone input convex neural networks (SOC-ICNNs), which recovers exact subdifferentials from optimal dual multipliers of an equivalent parametric second-order cone program. DCI combines network and feasible-set geometry to produce exact stationarity certificates and tangent common descent directions, using local curvature for Newton acceleration with an exact proximal safeguard, and it establishes global convergence plus local quadratic convergence near structurally nondegenerate interior minimizers. ICNNs are widely used to learn convex objectives whose minimizers define decisions, so reliable and efficient optimization at inference is central to their deployment in control, reinforcement learning, and structured prediction. By providing exact subdifferential recovery and certified Newton-accelerated optimization with global convergence guarantees, DCI addresses a key weakness of standard automatic differentiation at nonsmooth inputs, potentially improving reliability for optimization and ML researchers working with convex models. The method exploits the exact representation of SOC-ICNNs as value functions of parametric second-order cone programs, deriving explicit Hessians on smooth regions and full subdifferentials at nonsmooth points from dual multipliers. Local quadratic convergence is only guaranteed under standard regularity conditions near structurally nondegenerate interior minimizers, and code is available at an anonymous repository (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DCI-ICNN-507D/).

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Input convex neural networks (ICNNs) are neural architectures whose parameters are constrained so that the output is a convex function of the inputs, making them attractive for learning convex objectives in optimization-based decision making. Second-order cone programming (SOCP) is a class of convex optimization problems with constraints involving Euclidean norms, and SOC-ICNNs are ICNNs that can be represented exactly as value functions of parametric SOCPs. In convex analysis, the subdifferential generalizes the gradient to nonsmooth convex functions, and automatic differentiation typically returns only a single derivative rather than the full subdifferential needed to characterize optimality and descent directions.

## [ReForge Refines Merged Models via Anchor-Regularized Bayesian Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12843) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ReForge introduces a bilevel optimization framework that refines merged models using anchor-regularized Bayesian linear regression, yielding a closed-form MAP estimate from unlabeled calibration activations. It also offers a data-free variant that replaces activation statistics with task-vector Grams, and on 20-task ViT-B/32 it improves the strongest baseline ISO-CTS from 77.6% to 82.8% (data-assisted) and 81.5% (data-free). Model merging is a practical alternative to multi-task learning when joint retraining is infeasible, but existing methods rarely exploit strong merged models as priors for further refinement. ReForge's consistent gains across vision and language benchmarks suggest it could become a plug-and-play refinement step that makes merged models competitive with individually trained experts. The inner level produces a closed-form MAP estimate, while the outer level uses Bayesian optimization to jointly select heterogeneous regularization strengths and assembly scales on held-out validation data. On eight-task ViT-L/14, the data-assisted variant reaches 95.1% mean accuracy, close to the 95.8% of individual task experts, though the data-free variant trades some accuracy for eliminating calibration examples.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Model merging combines multiple task-specific expert models into a single model without joint retraining, offering a practical alternative to multi-task learning when data access or computational budget is limited. Bilevel optimization nests one optimization problem within another, with an upper-level and a lower-level task, and Bayesian linear regression provides a probabilistic way to obtain posterior estimates of regression coefficients. ReForge builds on these ideas by using a merged model as an anchor-centered prior and refining it module-wise.

## [LEAF: A Living Benchmark for Event-Augmented Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16358) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced LEAF, the first living benchmark for event-augmented forecasting tasks covering trend, event, and time series forecasting, which combines a recursive retrieval agent with dual-agent cross-validation to gather temporally aligned auxiliary context. An audit of 500 tasks by 47 domain specialists showed the pipeline reduced future information leakage from 8.6% to 1.6%, and evaluations of 16 frontier proprietary and open-weight models confirmed LLMs can extract signals from verified events to improve trend and event forecasting. This matters because LLM forecasting evaluations are often compromised by pre-training data contamination and look-ahead leakage, making reported predictive capabilities unreliable. LEAF provides a rigorously audited, expert-validated benchmark that could become a standard for measuring genuine forecasting ability in a fast-growing research area. The benchmark's recursive retrieval agent system and dual-agent cross-validation are designed to gather comprehensive, relevant, and temporally aligned auxiliary context, while the expert audit quantified leakage reduction across 500 tasks. The evaluation covered 16 frontier proprietary and open-weight models, showing LLMs benefit most on trend and event forecasting when events are verified.

**Background**: Event-augmented forecasting uses auxiliary textual events, such as news or reports, alongside time series data to improve predictions. Look-ahead leakage occurs when future information accidentally enters training or evaluation, producing overly optimistic performance estimates, and pre-training data contamination similarly inflates LLM results. A living benchmark is one that is continuously updated to avoid models memorizing static test sets.

## [HINT-SD Targets Failure Spans for Efficient Long-Horizon Agent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17873) ⭐️ 7.0/10

HINT-SD is a targeted self-distillation framework that uses full-trajectory hindsight to identify failure-relevant actions and applies feedback-conditioned distillation only to those specific action spans. On BFCL v3 and AppWorld, it outperforms the dense per-turn feedback baseline by up to 13.60 percentage points on average while reducing time per training step by 2.26×. This work addresses a core inefficiency in training long-horizon LLM agents with reinforcement learning, where sparse outcome rewards make it hard to assign credit to intermediate actions. By showing that selecting where to distill matters more than distilling everywhere, it offers a more scalable path to building capable multi-turn agents. The method avoids generating feedback at every turn, which is wasteful when many intermediate turns are already successful or neutral, and instead targets only the action spans that contributed to failure. This targeted supervision avoids the misalignment problem of applying feedback at a fixed or arbitrary turn.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Long-horizon LLM agents must complete tasks over many turns of interaction with tools and environments, and reinforcement learning typically provides only a sparse reward at the end indicating success or failure. Self-distillation lets the same policy act as a teacher under different contexts to generate richer supervision, but applying it uniformly across all turns is costly and often misaligned with the actions that actually caused failure. BFCL v3 is Berkeley's function-calling benchmark for multi-turn, multi-step tool use, and AppWorld is a benchmark for interactive agent tasks.

## [EchoDistill Boosts Noise Robustness in Large Audio Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23954) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose EchoDistill, a noisy-to-clean self-distillation framework that uses clean audio as privileged information during post-training to make Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) more robust to acoustic noise. Across three LALM backbones and three audio domains at -10dB, it improves average noisy-input accuracy by 1.63 percentage points over the strongest baseline, raising Qwen2.5-Omni from 59.33% to 62.94% while also improving clean-audio accuracy from 76.56% to 77.56%. Acoustic noise is a persistent weakness of audio-language models, causing unreliable responses in real-world deployments such as voice assistants and audio understanding systems. Because only the student model is retained at inference, EchoDistill delivers these robustness gains without any additional inference cost, making it practical for deployment across diverse backbones and domains. EchoDistill combines masked response-token distillation, task-gated consistency shaping, and teacher-referenced group-relative optimization to align noisy-input generation with clean-conditioned semantics. Ablations show that replacing matched audio with random, shuffled, or silent inputs reduces accuracy by 3.08-6.42 points, but the gains do not reliably extend to non-additive distortions.

Self-distillation is a family of techniques in which a model distills knowledge within itself, using its own internal structure or predictions rather than an external teacher model. Emergency-tier information was linearly decodable from vignette representations with ROC-AUC 0.95–1.00 under both formats with no significant format difference, but was attenuated at the decision token; option-order shuffles ruled out simple positional bias, and cases that differed between formats were usually one severity tier apart. ## [SCAP: Stiefel Cross-Attention Pooling Breaks SPDNet Capacity Ceiling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31043) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper identifies a capacity ceiling in stacked BiMap layers with ReEig nonlinearity on SPD manifolds, showing that on real preconditioned EEG data ReEig rarely activates and the stack behaves as a single layer regardless of depth. It proposes SCAP (Stiefel Cross-Attention Pool), a layer that combines a pool of K experts into a sample-specific bilinear map via cross-attention, and demonstrates significant balanced-accuracy gains over fixed-filter SPDNet on all five cross-domain EEG motor-imagery datasets. This addresses a fundamental limitation in geometric deep learning on SPD manifolds, where depth has long failed to deliver the expected representational gains, and offers a principled routing mechanism that could improve domain adaptation and SPD network design. The results suggest that sample-specific bilinear maps can escape the fixed-filter ceiling, with potential impact on EEG-based brain-computer interfaces and other SPD-based applications. The authors prove that when domains share no discriminative directions, a single filter has a capacity ceiling and cannot align every domain at once, and they show SCAP matches a per-domain filter bank to first order with fewer experts than domains when domain-optimal filters span few directions near a shared tangent-space basepoint. Naively trained routing can collapse to a fixed filter, so they adapt three mechanisms to mitigate this, and SCAP matches or exceeds three domain-adaptive baselines on four out of five datasets.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrices are widely used as rich descriptors (e.g., region covariances) and their Riemannian geometry provides a strong inductive bias for deep networks. SPDNet-style architectures stack BiMap layers (which perform bilinear transformations) with ReEig nonlinearity (eigenvalue clamping) and LogEig for classification, but the ReEig activation often fails to add capacity. The Stiefel manifold, the set of orthonormal k-frames, provides the geometric structure for the filters used in SCAP's cross-attention routing.

A new arXiv paper (2606.00435v5) proposes Text-Conditioned Layer-wise Internal Alignment (TC-LIA), a training-free, model-agnostic method that detects when vision-language models produce confident answers without visual evidence — a failure mode called 'mirage.' On 19,004 samples across 10 VQA domains and 14 state-of-the-art VLMs, base mirage rates of 57.3–75.0% were cut to 7.5% by TC-LIA alone, and to 5.9–7.2% when combined with an optional ensemble. By enabling pre-release filtering of unreliable VLM outputs without any label-specific training, TC-LIA offers a practical, deployable safeguard for real-world VLM applications. TC-LIA tracks question-image alignment across layers of a frozen CLIP ViT-H/14 encoder, summarizing patch-text alignment via final similarity, late-layer top-k alignment, early-to-late gain, and slope. It achieves 83.5% Related/Unrelated/Blank-Noise classification accuracy alone, and an ensemble with blank/noise detection, domain routing, and VLM self-assessment reaches 84.5–88.4% accuracy; notably, an ensemble trained on a single backbone transfers to unseen backbones within 0.7% accuracy points across 13 held-out VLMs.

## [ENPO Fixes Exponential Exploration Cost in Nash Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01382) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2606.01382v2) proves that standard iterative Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF) can suffer an exponential dependence on the inverse KL-regularization parameter, meaning implicit exploration through policy updates is insufficient. The authors propose Exploratory Nash Preference Optimization (ENPO), which combines SFT-type regularization with adversarial policy exploration, and further introduce Bonus-Explorer ENPO (BENPO) with an O(log T) regret bound and Direct ENPO (DENPO), a practical fine-tuning variant that improves over RLHF and NLHF baselines on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. This work strengthens the theoretical foundations of preference alignment for LLMs by showing why simple iterative NLHF methods can be sample-inefficient and how to fix it without minimax oracles or explicit preference-model estimation. It matters for researchers and practitioners building RLHF/NLHF pipelines, since DENPO offers a practical path to more efficient fine-tuning when human preferences are non-transitive. The paper shows standard iterative NLHF can incur exponential dependence on the inverse KL-regularization parameter, while ENPO removes this dependence without minimax oracles or explicit preference-model estimation; BENPO uses additional oracles to achieve an O(log T) regret bound. Experiments with Llama-3-8B-Instruct show consistent improvements over evaluated RLHF and NLHF baselines across multiple benchmarks, though the work is a preprint and its practical impact remains to be validated.

**Background**: Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF) reframes LLM alignment as a two-player zero-sum preference game and seeks a Nash equilibrium, which handles non-transitive human preferences better than reward-based RLHF. KL-regularization keeps the learned policy close to a reference policy and is central to RLHF efficiency, but its strength (the inverse KL-regularization parameter) can dramatically affect learning. Exploration—deliberately trying diverse policies—is what lets a learner discover good strategies, and this paper studies whether iterative NLHF explores enough on its own.

## [SovereignNegotiation-Bench Tests Personal AI Agents Against Agency Law Duties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02814) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced SovereignNegotiation-Bench, a controlled benchmark that operationalizes five duties from agency law—loyalty, obedience to actual authority, confidentiality, candor, and diligence—as deterministic checks on episode logs. It contains 1,764 paired scenarios across 18 consumer and peer-to-peer domains, each tested under 7 counterparty tactics, and evaluates 17 open-weight models whose faithful success ranges from 6% to 75%. As personal AI agents begin negotiating refunds, bills, and deposits on users' behalf, this benchmark shifts evaluation from whether a deal was struck to whether the agent honored its duties to the principal. It exposes that deal rate does not certify individual agreements—pooled over models, 48% of agreements breach at least one duty—highlighting risks for anyone deploying consumer-facing negotiation agents. The counterparty's economics are a fixed function of the agent's structured actions and detected disclosures, so a disclosed limit has a measurable causal price; rule-based agents achieve 92% faithful success, but a single disclosing sentence erases the entire negotiated surplus (0.70 to 0.00). Models disclosed the principal's reservation value in 2–80% of episodes, shared protected documents without approval in 2–23%, and followed injected instructions in 5–57% of injection episodes, with neither prompting nor a code-level guard substantially improving faithful success.

## [ELSA3D Unifies 3D Understanding and Generation via Elastic Semantic Anchoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06565) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ELSA3D introduces elastic semantic anchoring, combining a scale-aware octree tokenizer with sparse Anchor Tokens that route text cues to matched geometric scales in a single unified 3D backbone. It achieves state-of-the-art results on image-to-3D generation, text-to-3D generation, and 3D captioning while roughly halving FLOPs and inference latency versus its non-elastic version. ELSA3D's explicit, scale-matched anchoring could shape how future multimodal 3D systems balance precision and efficiency, affecting researchers and developers building text-driven 3D asset pipelines. The model uses a lightweight per-block router that decides which text tokens instantiate anchors at which geometric scale, keeping cross-modal interaction sparse yet precise. The reported gains come from an arXiv preprint (2607.06565v2) and have not yet been independently validated or discussed by the community.

## [Study Identifies 'Delegation Regret' in General-Purpose AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18257) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A controlled study with 20 university students using the OpenClaw general-purpose AI agent found that users experience 'delegation regret' when the agent acts beyond what they would have authorized, even if the action succeeds. The study also found that users calibrate trust per task rather than per agent, demanding confirmation for irreversible, externally visible actions. This research introduces delegation regret as a distinct failure mode in human-agent interaction, highlighting that user dissatisfaction can stem from unauthorized action rather than incorrect output. The findings have implications for designing AI agents that expose action boundaries, support per-task autonomy policies, and separate advisory output from agentic execution. The study measured trust, perceived control, transparency, supervision burden, and approval preference on 5-point Likert scales across five daily tasks varying in privacy, stakes, and reversibility. The moderate-stakes email task triggered the sharpest drop in trust (M = 3.10) and highest demand for approval (M = 4.65), while a high-stakes but verifiable task did not produce the same response.

## [Early Detection of Distributed Backdoors in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24893) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv characterization study (arXiv:2607.24893v2) builds a working distributed backdoor attack on a hierarchical multi-agent LLM system, where several poisoned tools each hide one encrypted fragment that is reassembled and executed after the run. The authors report that a prefix detector flags 99.5% of successful attacks once fragment injection begins, with a median of twelve steps remaining and an out-of-fold false-alarm rate of about 1% on uninjected runs. This is a timely and under-explored security problem: per-step safety checks that judge each action in isolation may fail to recognize a complete distributed payload that no single agent ever holds in full. The finding that alarms could enable an abort before assembly on nearly every successful attack has direct implications for AI safety and the deployment of multi-agent LLM systems. The study runs benign and attacked conditions across five language models and two tool environments, recording when each fragment is injected and when the payload is assembled and executed. Generic zero-shot and behavior-trained detectors fail to separate unsafe from safe runs, and the detectors that do work lean partly on removable surface cues — chiefly the ciphertext's length and entropy; removing those cues delays detection and makes cross-environment transfer much harder, though a model fine-tuned on raw text recovers part of the loss.

## [Addressable Global Memory to Fix Oversquashing in Message Passing Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02709) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.02709v2) proposes addressable and support-aware global memory mechanisms for message passing networks, showing that multiplicative write/read maps can provide M selectable memory rows using only O(log M) address-code dimensions under constant-margin address codes. On Two-Radius and Tree-NeighborsMatch tasks, both addressable realizations solve the controlled tasks through depth 5, while pooled virtual nodes of comparable or larger size reach only about 10.6%. Oversquashing is a well-known failure mode of message-passing graph neural networks, and this work shows that the standard virtual-node shortcut can itself become a bottleneck when many nodes share one global state. By making global memory addressable and support-aware, the approach offers a principled way to preserve long-range information flow, which could benefit researchers working on graph transformers, graph rewiring, and long-range graph learning. The paper formalizes two properties of global memory: addressability, where constant-margin address codes plus a margin-amplifying nonlinearity allow M selectable rows with O(log M) dimensions, and support awareness, where a learned private anchor supplies a self-key reference for normalized cross-attention so reads stay bounded and the matching source mass is exposed. Cross-attention slots and a constrained ELU+1 bilinear memory both satisfy these conditions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs) propagate information between neighboring nodes, but as the number of hops grows, information from many distant nodes gets compressed into fixed-size vectors, a problem known as oversquashing. Virtual nodes are a common mitigation: they act as a global hub so that any node can reach any other in two hops instead of many. However, when all nodes read and write to a single shared global state, that hub can become an information bottleneck, which is the issue this paper addresses.

A new arXiv paper (2608.06481v2) proposes a curriculum-driven framework that tightly couples scenario-based Evolution Strategy with Statistical Model Checking in a closed loop, co-optimizing neural policies while progressively enlarging their verified safe operating region. This paper proposes a fine-tuning-based Stratified Consistency Distillation approach that generates K logical translations per input using a frontier LLM, clusters them by semantic equivalence, and selects pseudo-labels via entropy-based strategies (majority voting, LLM-as-a-Judge, or unification/abstention) to fine-tune a smaller model. Experiments show significant and consistent improvements in Pass@K and a novel Equivalent Logical Similarity metric. This work addresses a key bottleneck in neurosymbolic reasoning—the accuracy of translating natural language into logical formulas—by moving beyond prompt engineering to a scalable fine-tuning approach. If validated, it could make neurosymbolic systems more robust and easier to deploy across domains and input formats. The method uses entropy thresholds to route examples: low entropy uses majority voting, medium entropy uses LLM-as-a-Judge, and high entropy uses unification or abstention. The paper is a preprint (arXiv:2608.30258v3) without peer review, and no community discussion is available.

## [Outcome-Only LLM Judges Fail on Silent Agent Faults](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00038) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.00038v2) introduces 'paired discrimination' — a judge's flag rate on faulty runs minus its flag rate on the clean runs they were derived from — and shows that a 14B outcome-only judge scoring 34%–76% recall on four reply-unchanged fault types actually has zero paired discrimination, meaning that recall is simply its flag rate on clean runs. The authors release a deterministic support-desk testbed with 400 exactly labeled trajectories, a scripted oracle, and a one-step fault injector, along with raw verdicts and an analysis pipeline. This work exposes a fundamental flaw in the widely used LLM-as-judge evaluation paradigm for agent trajectories: high recall can be an artifact of a judge's tendency to flag anything, not evidence of real detection ability. It matters for anyone building or auditing agent evaluation pipelines, since inflated recall metrics could mask silent failures that never surface in the final reply but still corrupt agent behavior. Splitting faults by whether they break the environment outcome does not fix the problem: the judge's loud recall of 84% corresponds to a paired +0.393, while its silent recall of 45% is only a paired +0.048, both driven by the two fault types that change the reply. When told to check each step, the same model flags every fault of the four reply-unchanged types and 0 of 100 clean runs (95% CI up to 3.6%), but it still fails to reliably check the reply itself — of four invented promises it flags one every time and the other three only once in 42 faults.

Fault injection is a testing technique that deliberately introduces errors into otherwise correct runs so that a judge's detection ability can be measured against known ground truth.

## [Suan: Gradient-Level Preference Optimization for LLM Safety Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08634) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.08634v2) introduces Suan, a preference optimization algorithm that formulates its objective directly at the gradient level rather than through the standard variational derivation. The authors report that Suan achieves superior safety alignment across multiple baselines and benchmarks while fully preserving response utility. Safety alignment in open-weight LLMs often degrades general quality and causes over-refusal, so an algorithm that improves safety without hurting utility could make open models more competitive with proprietary systems. The gradient-level formulation also offers more interpretable and robust training dynamics, which matters for the broader AI alignment and safety guardrail community. The key technical distinction is that Suan bypasses the standard variational derivation used by most preference optimization methods and instead defines the objective at the gradient level, yielding more interpretable training dynamics. The abstract claims extensive evaluation against competitive baselines, but as a preprint it has not yet undergone peer review and no code or community discussion is mentioned.

## [Coding Agents Ignore Safety Constraints in Robot Control, Paper Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20822) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.20822v2) evaluates coding agents — language models that write robot controllers as programs — under explicit safety constraints, and finds that agents collide with forbidden obstacles in most cases because task completion is treated as the sole objective. The authors propose SafeHarness, an obstacle-aware harness with route planning and contact execution modules, which achieves 81.2% task success and 91.9% collision avoidance with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previous state of the art by 13.7 and 23.0 points. This work identifies a novel and important safety failure mode in LLM-driven robotics: the model perceives the obstacle and the prompt forbids contact, yet the stated constraint never becomes a planning priority. As coding agents become a mainstream paradigm for robot manipulation without robot-specific training, this finding suggests that safe deployment requires explicit harnesses rather than relying on model reasoning or prompt instructions alone. The failure is located in planning rather than perception or instruction: along the route phase the model has no notion of a clearing route and no replanning once a chosen route becomes infeasible, and at the contact-rich moment it is unaware that contact execution is bounded by the same constraint. SafeHarness addresses this by grounding objects as bounding boxes and drawing candidate routes as waypoint sequences that the agent plans, verifies, and replans before execution, while obstacle-aware contact execution selects contact positions that avoid the obstacle.

## [RL Generalization Gaps Need a Random Policy Floor, Paper Argues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32532) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.32532v2) argues that reinforcement learning generalization gaps—training return minus held-out return—should be measured against a random floor: the return of a uniform-random policy on the same levels under the same evaluation harness. Testing PPO on eight ProcGen environments at a compute-limited budget (8M steps, 16 parallel environments, with three games extended to 25M), the authors show the floor changes what standard numbers mean, and an audit of twelve ProcGen codebases finds nine sample test-time actions with no explicit choice at the evaluation call site. The findings suggest that widely reported RL generalization gaps may be misleading without a reference point, since the test-time action rule alone can flip which policy appears better. This has direct implications for how RL researchers and practitioners report benchmark results on ProcGen and similar procedurally generated suites, and could push the field toward more rigorous evaluation standards. In the miner environment, the sampled policy scores 5.1x the floor on held-out levels while its argmax scores below the floor in every run, and greedy evaluation places two environments significantly below the floor. Raw policy entropy flags six of eight environments as non-converged, but 32-66% of that entropy lies on actions with identical effects; measured against the floor, five of eight sampled policies are clearly above it on held-out levels while heist's is not distinguishable from it.

## [MaskCoFT: Co-Adaptive Fine-Tuning for Memory-Efficient MoE Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34077) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MaskCoFT introduces a masked co-adaptive fine-tuning method that jointly trains routers and experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models using only the cross-entropy loss, with a learnable binary mask restricting each layer's Top-K routing to a subset of experts during fine-tuning. Evaluated on Mixtral-8x7B and DeepSeek-V2-Lite, it reduces expert fetches per token by 23.7% and 10.1%, cuts time per output token by up to 16.4% and 5.5% in real offloading systems, and improves average accuracy over nine benchmarks by 0.92 and 0.53 points. This work addresses a key bottleneck in deploying large MoE models on memory-constrained hardware, where decoding speed is limited by how many experts each token must fetch from host memory. By reshaping routing and letting experts adapt together, it offers a practical path to faster, more memory-efficient inference without sacrificing accuracy, which matters for anyone serving large MoE models on limited GPUs. The method simulates a GPU cache of 4 experts per layer for Mixtral-8x7B and 12 for DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and at inference the learned mask becomes a soft prior that re-ranks experts so every expert remains selectable. Unlike router-only fine-tuning, which keeps experts frozen, MaskCoFT lets experts adapt to the tokens redirected to them, though gains are measured under simulated cache settings rather than arbitrary hardware configurations.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models replace a single large feed-forward network with many smaller expert networks, and a router selects the Top-K experts for each token, enabling large parameter counts with less compute per token. Because expert weights can exceed a single GPU's memory, expert offloading keeps most experts in host memory and loads them on demand, making decoding speed depend on how many experts each token must fetch. Caching and prefetching help only as far as the routing allows, and router-only fine-tuning can reshape routing but leaves experts frozen.

The core detector and its compression port cleanly to both embedded targets, but the operators needed for long-range robustness survive only on the Jetson AGX Orin GPU, not on the Versal VCK190 DPU.

A new arXiv paper (2609.38516v2) introduces the concept of 'recursive social improvement' and tests whether self-improving LLM agents can learn from one another to improve the whole population. When models wrote and revised their own skills, observing peers helped one model find useful skills sooner and another spend less on private search, but neither outperformed independent learners at the same cost, and exchanges concentrated the population around fewer independent discoveries.

## [CRAFT Traces Causal Attention Heads Behind Medical VLM Safety Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38810) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38810v2) introduces CRAFT, a framework that localizes two safety failure modes in medical vision-language models to spatially disjoint populations of attention heads: 'arbitration heads' that let misleading text override correct image-based diagnoses, and 'brake heads' that control whether the model abstains when visual evidence is insufficient. The authors verify causality by excising these heads, showing that removing arbitration heads sharply reduces conflict-following with negligible degradation on clean inputs, while removing brake heads restores appropriate abstention under degraded visual evidence. This work extends mechanistic interpretability from unimodal text models into multimodal clinical settings, offering causal rather than correlational explanations for why medical VLMs can be dangerously misled by a single sentence or commit to answers without adequate evidence. Because the identified heads can be modulated without retraining and generalize across benchmarks and architectures, the findings could inform safer model design and targeted interventions for AI deployed in healthcare. The two failure modes are mechanistically separable: arbitration heads form a mid-to-deep wideband reflecting cross-layer evidence competition, while brake heads concentrate in a narrow middle-to-late layer band regulating evidence sufficiency and abstention. CRAFT localizes each failure mode to a minimal causal head set using dual criteria and verifies necessity and sufficiency through temporal probes and Tuned Lens trajectory analysis, with code released at github.com/zhcz328/CRAFT.

## [MintFlow: Minimal Trajectory Intervention for Constrained Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02260) ⭐️ 6.0/10

MintFlow introduces a training-free constrained sampling framework that enforces constraints by minimally perturbing an intermediate state of a pretrained flow trajectory, using an adjoint formulation to derive a closed-form perturbation and adaptively selecting the intervention time. Across generative vision and physical system modeling tasks, it achieves competitive constraint satisfaction while preserving the pretrained distribution substantially better than state-of-the-art constrained methods. This addresses a core trade-off in constrained generative modeling: existing samplers often displace samples far from the pretrained distribution when enforcing constraints, which can degrade sample quality and realism. By minimizing deviation while remaining training-free, MintFlow could make constrained generation more practical for scientific and engineering applications where both physical consistency and distributional fidelity matter. The method formulates constraint enforcement as a minimal perturbation of an intermediate flow state, keeping the pretrained flow field unchanged, and uses an adjoint formulation to obtain a closed-form perturbation that avoids expensive iterative optimization. It also adaptively selects the intervention time to balance the required perturbation magnitude against its amplification by the remaining flow.

**Background**: Flow matching is a generative modeling paradigm based on continuous normalizing flows that learns a time-dependent velocity field to transform noise into data samples, typically by solving an ordinary differential equation. Constrained sampling in generative models aims to produce samples that satisfy prescribed conditions such as observed measurements or physical laws, but often at the cost of moving away from the original data distribution. The adjoint state method is a numerical technique for efficiently computing gradients in optimization problems, and here it enables a closed-form solution for the minimal trajectory perturbation.

Seg-OPD uses an uncertainty metric to decide which student segments to replace with teacher redrafts, and it combines this segment-level preference objective with the original dense token-wise OPD loss rather than replacing it. Seg-OPD extends OPD by moving part of the supervision from individual tokens to whole reasoning segments, using teacher redrafts as explicit targets for revision.

## [ROUTEAUDIT: Contract-Conditioned Routing for Multi-Verifier Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02808) ⭐️ 6.0/10

ROUTEAUDIT proposes a contract-conditioned identification framework that formalizes verifier routing as a causal inference problem, introducing three measurable objects: a contract lattice, a policy-independent response tape, and request-level bounds. On 1,319 held-out task requests, the RLVR-static paired difference is +0.0068 with a request-paired interval of [0.0015, 0.0122], and controlled attribution recovery achieves route mean absolute error of 0.0011. This work addresses a fundamental fairness problem in adaptive multi-verifier systems, where endpoint quality-cost gaps are commonly used for comparison even when the verifier catalog, availability, or accounting changes with the policy. By providing a principled identification contract and attribution certificates, it enables fair, budgeted routing decisions that could improve resource allocation in AI verification pipelines. The framework commits paid observations and ledger events before the oracle join, returning an attribution certificate for each comparison. On two held-out raw-tail caches, matched static SF+SA equals the cascade, assigning apparent gains of 0.1797 and 0.1250 over full static to the verifier-set edge, and the RLVR-static paired difference has a training-seed-by-request hierarchical interval of [0.0006, 0.0131].

## [FSPO: Policy-Consistent Risk and Pareto-Feasible Control for Budgeted LLM RL Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02828) ⭐️ 6.0/10

FSPO introduces a feedback-state controller for budgeted LLM RL post-training that jointly addresses policy-consistent risk estimation, decision-conditioned calibration, and Pareto-feasible multi-resource control. Under a matched GRPO resource envelope, FSPO reaches 66.11% held-out and 59.43% OOD accuracy, compared with 64.47% and 57.03% for PB2, the strongest evaluated adaptive baseline. This work matters because adaptive LLM RL post-training typically changes multiple training actuators online, and existing methods struggle to keep risk estimates consistent with the deployed controller or to certify multi-resource feasibility. FSPO's joint treatment of these coupled issues could improve the reliability and budget efficiency of RL-based LLM post-training pipelines. FSPO combines a policy-consistent risk-to-go model whose Bellman target follows the same frozen controller used for future decisions, decision-conditioned trajectory calibration (DCTC) on cross-fitted trajectories, and a Pareto resource continuation certificate (PRCC) that admits an action only when a non-dominated cumulative reservation remains feasible over the residual horizon. In ablations, policy-consistent risk lowers selected-decision ECE from 0.108 to 0.053 under high behavior-deployment mismatch, DCTC lowers it from 0.039 to 0.022 at matched acceptance, PRCC removes false-feasible admissions on an 18-action catalog ($0.197\rightarrow0.000$), and enabling all three components reduces trajectory failure from 0.181 to 0.083.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 5, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning post-training for large language models adapts a pretrained model using reward signals, and recent systems adjust training actuators such as rollout temperature, group size, clipping, KL regularization, verifier allocation, and update budget online. The Bellman equation is a fundamental recursive relationship in RL that expresses the value of a state as the immediate reward plus the expected value of the next state, and it underpins risk-to-go and utility models. Pareto feasibility comes from multi-objective optimization, where a solution is Pareto efficient if no other feasible solution is better in all objectives; here it is used to certify that a multi-resource training continuation remains feasible.

## [Write-Time Summarization Policies Compared for Multi-Goal Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02897) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02897) presents a policy ablation comparing three write-time summarization strategies for multi-goal LLM agent memory: summarizing with no goal in view, writing one unified summary covering all goals, or writing one separate summary per goal and reading them together. Across several models and event streams with the read step held fixed, per-goal summaries won on relevance, completeness, and accuracy, while the all-goal summary performed worse than even the neutral summary written at a fraction of its budget. As LLM agents evolve into long-running assistants that must serve multiple standing user goals simultaneously, how memory is compressed at write time directly determines what information survives and what is permanently lost. This work suggests that goal-aware write-time summarization is a cheap, practical improvement over unified summarization, which has direct implications for the design of production agent memory systems. The study holds the read step constant so that only the write policy varies, isolating the effect of write-time interpretation. A notable finding is that summaries written for different goals overlap each other less than a summary overlaps a rewrite of itself, and that interpreting at write time pays off only for the specific goal that later queries the memory.

**Background**: LLM agents with long conversation histories cannot retain everything they have seen, so they compress past events into summaries that replace the original stream in the context window. This compression is not neutral: the choice of what to keep is made before it is known which of the user's standing goals will later need that information. Multi-goal agents are systems that must simultaneously serve several persistent user objectives, making the summarization policy a critical design decision.

The method requires no alarm safety labels for fitting and leaves the underlying monitor unchanged; it casts false-alarm auditing as a PU ranking problem where verified-safe non-alarmed trajectories serve as positives and alarms remain unlabeled. The key challenge is monitor-induced selection: observed safe references are accepted by the monitor, while hidden safe alarms are exactly those it incorrectly flags, making observed positives poorly representative.

## [CreateScore uses Bayesian routing to cut LLM CV screening costs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02972) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CreateScore introduces a domain-theory-informed Bayesian network that routes criterion-level CV screening decisions between a local 8B LLM and a 120B reference model, resolving 77.7% of decisions locally on 200 synthetic Data Science CVs. Routed escalation reduced token use by 65.2% and raised exact score agreement from 32.8% (8B alone) to 42.6%, though the uncertainty signal did not identify where the 8B model erred (AUROC 0.47). As organizations increasingly adopt LLMs for high-volume tasks like CV screening, the cost of querying large models for every decision becomes prohibitive. This work shows that Bayesian routing can substantially reduce costs while modestly improving accuracy, but also highlights that uncertainty-based routing may not reliably target errors, an important caveat for cascade system design. The system uses a hand-specified directed acyclic graph with Dirichlet-multinomial conditional probability tables to convert CV evidence into posterior uncertainty, with an escalation threshold calibrated on a training fold (target: 70% resolved locally) and then frozen. The evaluation is limited to 200 synthetic CVs across five criteria, and at n=61 the accuracy gain was not statistically distinguishable; the authors also document how an earlier evaluation was invalidated when truncated reasoning-model outputs were silently replaced by local labels.

A new arXiv paper introduces Ψ-Resilience, a model-free feature importance method that builds a class-disagreement landscape from class-conditional densities and uses 0-dimensional persistence of this 1D signal to produce a robustness-scaled importance score. On synthetic data with known ground truth it achieves Spearman rank correlations up to 0.8, and on real datasets it agrees with SHAP and mutual information with correlations up to 0.9. Feature importance is central to interpretable machine learning, but most popular methods such as SHAP depend on a trained predictive model and its behavior. By deriving importance directly from the data distribution and making the score auditable through explicit 1D landscapes and persistence, Ψ-Resilience offers a distribution-level alternative that could be useful for model auditing, fairness checks, and settings where no reliable model is available. The method estimates class-conditional densities, takes their pointwise absolute difference along each feature axis to form a class-disagreement landscape, and then aggregates only topological features that survive perturbations up to a user-set robustness scale. This makes the importance score context-dependent and inherently auditable, though the choice of robustness scale and density estimation quality remain practical considerations.

The paper warns that truncated top-k teacher scores should not be treated as full 60-class soft targets for KL distillation, since zeroing untruncated classes destroys the dark knowledge soft-label distillation depends on and introduces systematic bias rather than a harmless sparse approximation.

The paper introduces Safe Variance-Adaptive Exploration (SVAE), an algorithm for episodic tabular constrained Markov decision processes with step-wise safety constraints. SVAE learns candidate safe subgraphs and performs variance-adaptive optimistic planning within them, achieving cumulative regret of order Õ(√(SAH min{V_Σ, K Var*}) + S√(AH³ min{K, C}) + S²AH²) over K episodes, along with a matching lower bound. This is a solid theoretical contribution to constrained reinforcement learning, providing the first instance-dependent regret bounds for CMDPs with step-wise constraints. It advances the theoretical understanding of safe exploration and could inform the design of more efficient safe RL algorithms. The regret bound depends on instance-specific quantities: Var* (maximum return variance among safe policies), V_Σ (variance accumulated before the first unsafe action), and C (statistical complexity of eliminating incorrectly safe actions). SVAE also achieves Õ(H√(SAK) + S²AH²) step-wise constraint violation and a gap-dependent violation bound polylogarithmic in K, with a lower bound proving these dependencies are unavoidable.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.02868) proposes a distributionally robust framework for survival analysis that jointly addresses latent subpopulation shift and outlier contamination. The method uses an alternating minimization-maximization algorithm, with outer updates derived from the KKT conditions of the inner maximization, and is evaluated on simulated data plus two survival benchmarks. In heterogeneous populations, a survival model that performs well on average can still fail badly on specific subpopulations, and this problem is worsened when training data contain outliers. By improving worst-group performance while keeping overall performance competitive, this work could make survival models more reliable in high-stakes applications such as clinical risk prediction. The formulation directly accommodates non-decomposable survival losses while preserving interactions across samples, including the risk-set structure of the Cox negative partial log-likelihood. Experiments show the method stabilizes training under contamination and substantially improves worst-group performance for both linear and nonlinear survival models.

LiBRA (Latent In-band Bidirectional Removal Attack) is a new attack that removes image watermarks by guiding average decoding confidence toward random guessing from either direction, rather than pushing the decoded watermark toward inversion. It makes bounded changes in a public autoencoder's latent space and verifies removal with an exact two-sided binomial test instead of assuming the confidence target guarantees success. This matters because watermarking is a key mechanism for source attribution of AI-generated images, and LiBRA exposes a weakness in inversion-based removal defenses by showing that an inverted watermark can remain detectable. It highlights the need for watermarking schemes that resist detection-aware latent-space attacks while preserving image quality. LiBRA assumes access to the watermark key and decoder, makes bounded changes in a public autoencoder's latent space, and optionally uses a frequency-guided mask to limit where changes occur. Leaving individual bits flexible allows image-quality constraints to favor less damaging changes, and removal is verified with an exact two-sided binomial test.

A new arXiv paper (2610.03475) theoretically proves that a single state-augmented policy can match the performance of any multi-policy solution in phase-structured reinforcement learning, but shows that practical outcomes depend on function approximation, learning, and optimization processes. The authors propose a regime-based phase decomposition method that uses the ratio of transient dynamics duration to quasi-stationary period duration to predict which approach will perform better. This work resolves a puzzling empirical observation in reinforcement learning — that multi-policy approaches sometimes outperform a single shared policy despite theoretical equivalence — by identifying the practical factors that drive the gap. It gives practitioners a principled way to decide between single-policy and multi-policy designs for non-stationary tasks such as robotics, autonomous driving, and clinical treatment planning. The paper validates four hypotheses through numerical experiments: longer phase durations favor multi-policies, greater heterogeneity between phases burdens a single policy, multi-policies require sufficient data per phase, and environment-specific transition dynamics between phases affect which policy is preferable. The proposed regime-based decomposition hinges on comparing the duration of transient system dynamics to the duration of the quasi-stationary period.

A new arXiv paper (2610.03577) introduces AutoTarget, a method that selects which tensor to cache in few-step Diffusion Transformers by measuring the reuse error for a given model, solver, and reuse schedule. It uses a small set of uncached calibration runs to rank candidate tensors and picks the one with the lowest error, with core code released on GitHub. Caching is a training-free way to cut the many costly DiT forward passes needed per sample, and it becomes more error-prone after step distillation widens the gap between adjacent steps. AutoTarget makes cache target selection systematic and solver-aware, which could improve sampling efficiency for practitioners deploying distilled image and video DiTs. The paper analyzes how an error at one reuse step propagates to the final sample, and for Euler sampling it identifies cache targets that yield the same trajectory while explaining why a stored solver update may not. Experiments on distilled image and video DiTs (including PixArt-LCM and FLUX.1-schnell) show the best cache target varies with model, resolution, and solver, and that AutoTarget's calibration ranking matches held-out cached runs while reducing DiT evaluations and cache storage.

Two common accelerations are step distillation, which reduces the number of sampling steps (often to a few), and caching, which skips some DiT evaluations by reusing a tensor computed at an earlier step. A new arXiv paper places a PPO agent in an analytically solved continuous-time broker-trader game, deriving a finite-step reward from the broker's continuous-time payoff. It finds that with zero uninformed order flow PPO approaches the reference action, but with stochastic uninformed flow PPO-FFNN and PPO-LSTM remain inaccurate even though supervised learning confirms their actors can represent the correct action. The results show that a correct reward signal is not sufficient for accurate reinforcement learning in financial optimal control, and that the critic's inability to rank nearby actions is a key failure mode. This has implications for anyone applying deep RL to trading or market-making, and suggests analytically solved models can serve as diagnostic benchmarks. Under partial information, a causal certainty-equivalent controller based on observable history stays close to the reference while PPO has larger errors and lower payoffs; freezing the analytical policy and training PPO to adapt after halving execution cost closes only 2.22% of the gap to the changed-cost reference.
